New Accelerated Past-Extragradient Methods with Variance Reduction for Generalized Equations

Quoc Tran-Dinh and Nghia Nguyen-Trung
Abstract

We develop a novel past-extragradient-type algorithmic framework, combining both Nesterov’s acceleration and variance-reduction techniques, to solve a class of generalized equations involving possibly nonmonotone operators in data-driven applications. Our framework covers a wide class of stochastic variance-reduced schemes, including mini-batching and both unbiased and biased control-variate estimators. We establish that our method achieves 𝒪⁡(1/k2)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k^{2}\big) convergence rates in expectation for the squared norm of the residual under Lipschitz continuity and a “co-hypomonotonicity-type” assumption, significantly improving upon non-accelerated counterparts by a factor of 1/k1/k. We also prove faster o⁡(1/k2)o\big(1/k^{2}\big) convergence rates, both in expectation and almost surely. In addition, we show that the sequence of iterates generated by our method almost surely converges to a solution of the underlying problem. We demonstrate the applicability of our method using general error approximation criteria, covering mini-batch stochastic estimators as well as three well-known control variate estimators: Loopless SVRG, SAGA, and Loopless SARAH. The resulting three variants attain significantly better oracle complexities than existing methods. We validate our framework and theoretical results through three numerical examples. The numerical results illustrate promising performance of our accelerated method over its non-accelerated counterparts.

1 Introduction.

The goal of this paper is to develop a novel accelerated past-extragradient-type framework with both unbiased and biased variance reduction techniques to solve the following possibly nonmonotone generalized equation:

Find x⋆∈ℝp such that: 0∈Φ​x⋆ with Φ​x:=G​x+T​x,{\textrm{Find $x^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that:~ $0\in\Phi{x}^{\star}$ with $\Phi{x}:=G{x}+Tx$},}\vskip-2.15277pt (GE)

where G:ℝp→ℝpG:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} is a single-valued mapping and T:ℝp⇉ℝpT:\mathbb{R}^{p}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^{p} is a possibly multivalued mapping. Throughout this paper, we assume that zer⁡(Φ):={x⋆∈ℝp:0∈Φ​x⋆}≠∅\mathrm{zer}(\Phi):=\{x^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:0\in\Phi{x}^{\star}\}\neq\emptyset, i.e., (GE) has a solution.

Following [95], we refer to (GE) as a composite generalized equation, but it is also known as a composite [non]linear inclusion, see [11]. In particular, if T=0T=0, then (GE) reduces to the following [non]linear equation (also known as a root-finding problem):

Find x⋆∈ℝp such that: G​x⋆=0.{\textrm{Find $x^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that:~ $Gx^{\star}=0$}.}\vskip-2.15277pt (NE)

This equation is equivalent to the following fixed-point problem:

Find x⋆∈ℝp such that x⋆=F​x⋆, where F​x:=x−λ​G​x for any λ>0.{\textrm{Find $x^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ such that $x^{\star}=Fx^{\star}$, where $Fx:=x-\lambda Gx$ for any $\lambda>0$}.}\vskip-2.15277pt (FP)

However, under appropriate conditions (e.g., maximal [co-hypo]monotonicity of TT), we can reformulate (GE) equivalently as (NE) using, e.g., a forward-backward splitting, backward-forward splitting, or Tseng’s forward-backward-forward splitting operator, see, e.g., [11, 102]. Under such conditions, we have the following relations: (GE) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (NE) ⇔\Leftrightarrow (FP).

Problem (GE) looks simple, but it is well-known that (GE) covers the optimality conditions of unconstrained and constrained minimization, minimax, and [mixed] variational inequality problems. It also comprises Nash equilibrium problems in economics [41].

1.1.\mathrm{1.1.} Our problem classes and assumptions. Before specifying our assumptions, we highlight that we will focus on two classes of (GE) as follows:

  1. 1.

    Class 1. GG is LL-Lipschitz continuous and G+TG+T is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone, i.e., GG satisfies Assumption 1 with α=1\alpha=1 and G+TG+T satisfies Assumption 1 below with ρn≥0\rho_{n}\geq 0 and ρc=0\rho_{c}=0.

  2. 2.

    Class 2. GG satisfies Assumption 1 with any α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) and G+TG+T satisfies both Assumption 1 and Assumption 1 below with ρn≥0\rho_{n}\geq 0 and ρc>0\rho_{c}>0.

In both classes, we assume that GG is not directly accessible and that we have access only to an unbiased stochastic oracle 𝐆\mathbf{G} of GG. More specifically, we impose the following assumptions.

{assumption}

[Unbiased oracle]​​​​​ GG is equipped with an unbiased stochastic oracle 𝐆\mathbf{G} as

G​x=𝔼ξ​[𝐆⁡(x,ξ)],∀x∈ℝp,{Gx=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)\big],\quad\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{p},}\vskip-2.15277pt (1)

where ξ\xi is a random variable on a given probability space (Ω,Σ,ℙ)(\Omega,\Sigma,\mathbb{P}) and 𝔼ξ​[𝐆⁡(⋅,ξ)]=∫Ω𝐆⁡(⋅,ξ)​ℙ​(𝑑ξ)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\mathbf{G}(\cdot,\xi)]=\int_{\Omega}\mathbf{G}(\cdot,\xi)\mathbb{P}(d\xi). Moreover, there exists σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 such that 𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−G​x‖2]≤σ2\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-Gx\|^{2}\big]\leq\sigma^{2}. Assumption 1 is widely used in the literature, especially in data-driven optimization applications, see, e.g., [63, 81]. In particular, if we choose Ω=[n]:={1,⋯,n}\Omega=[n]:=\{1,\cdots,n\}, ℙ⁡(ξ=i)=1n\mathbb{P}(\xi=i)=\frac{1}{n} for all i∈Ωi\in\Omega, and 𝐆⁡(x,ξ):=Gξ​x\mathbf{G}(x,\xi):=G_{\xi}x with Gi:ℝp→ℝpG_{i}:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} for i∈[n]i\in[n] are single-valued mappings, then GG becomes

G​x=𝔼ξ​[𝐆⁡(x,ξ)]=∑i=1nℙ⁡(ξ=i)​𝐆​(x,i)=1n​∑i=1nGi​x.{Gx=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}(\xi=i)\mathbf{G}(x,i)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}G_{i}x.}\vskip-2.15277pt (2)

This is called a finite-sum representation. It can also be obtained by sample average approximation techniques. In many applications, nn is very large so that evaluating GG is expensive or even infeasible.

{assumption}

[Lipschitz continuity-type] There exist two constants L∈(0,+∞)L\in(0,+\infty) and α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] such that for all x,y∈ℝpx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, we have

α​‖G​x−G​y‖2+(1−α)​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]≤L2​‖x−y‖2.{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\alpha\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}+(1-\alpha)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]\leq L^{2}\|x-y\|^{2}.\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt (3)

Note that we allow α=0\alpha=0 and α=1\alpha=1 in Assumption 1. If α=1\alpha=1, then (3) reduces to ‖G​x−G​y‖≤L​‖x−y‖\|Gx-Gy\|\leq L\|x-y\|, showing that GG is LL-Lipschitz continuous. If α=0\alpha=0, then (3) becomes 𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]≤L2​‖x−y‖2\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]\leq L^{2}\|x-y\|^{2}, showing that GG is LL-Lipschitz continuous in expectation. While the former is standard in classical stochastic approximation methods, the latter condition is often used in variance-reduction algorithms with control variate techniques, especially in optimization, see, e.g., [38, 85, 88, 106]. In fact, (3) is a convex combination of these two extreme cases. Note that ‖G​x−G​y‖2=‖𝔼ξ​[𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)]‖2≤𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}=\|\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\big]\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big] by Jensen’s inequality, (3) implies ‖G​x−G​y‖≤L​‖x−y‖\|Gx-Gy\|\leq L\|x-y\| for all x,y∈ℝpx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, i.e., GG is LL-Lipschitz continuous.

In the finite-sum setting (2), our condition (3) reduces to

α​‖G​x−G​y‖2+1−αn​∑i=1n‖Gi​x−Gi​y‖2≤L2​‖x−y‖2.{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\alpha\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}+\frac{1-\alpha}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|G_{i}x-G_{i}y\|^{2}\leq L^{2}\|x-y\|^{2}.\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt (4)

If α=0\alpha=0, then GG is said to be LL-average Lipschitz continuous.

{assumption}

[Weak Minty solution] There exists a solution x⋆∈zer⁡(Φ)x^{\star}\in\mathrm{zer}(\Phi) of (GE) and a constant ρ∗≥0\rho_{*}\geq 0 such that

⟨w,x−x⋆⟩≥−ρ∗∥w∥2,∀(x,w)∈gra(Φ).{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle w,x-x^{\star}\rangle\geq-\rho_{*}\|w\|^{2},\quad\forall(x,w)\in\mathrm{gra}(\Phi).\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt (5)

This assumption also covers a class of nonmonotone operators Φ\Phi and has been widely used in the literature in recent years, see, e.g., [37, 105] for examples. It is weaker than the so-called “star-monotonicity” of Φ\Phi (i.e., ρ∗=0\rho_{*}=0) used in some recent works, e.g., [45, 61].

{assumption}

[Co-hypomonotonicity-type] There exist ρn≥0\rho_{n}\geq 0 and ρc≥0\rho_{c}\geq 0 such that ρn≥ρc\rho_{n}\geq\rho_{c} and for all (x,wx),(y,wy)∈gra⁡(Φ)(x,w_{x}),(y,w_{y})\in\mathrm{gra}(\Phi), we have

⟨wx−wy,x−y⟩≥−ρn​‖wx−wy‖2+ρc​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2].{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle w_{x}-w_{y},x-y\rangle\geq-\rho_{n}\|w_{x}-w_{y}\|^{2}+\rho_{c}\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big].\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt (6)

The condition (6) in Assumption 1 looks technical and nonstandard. It deserves further discussion. Note that since we allow ρc=0\rho_{c}=0, (6) can reduce to

⟨wx−wy,x−y⟩≥−ρn​‖wx−wy‖2.{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle w_{x}-w_{y},x-y\rangle\geq-\rho_{n}\|w_{x}-w_{y}\|^{2}.\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt

This relation shows that Φ\Phi is ρn\rho_{n}-co-hypomonotone. Clearly, Assumption 1 includes ordinary co-hypomonotonicity as a special case and, when T=0T=0, also encompasses average co-coercive operators. To develop variance-reduction methods via control-variate techniques in Section 4, we will require ρc>0\rho_{c}>0. In the finite-sum setting (2), the condition (6) reduces to ⟨wx−wy,x−y⟩≥−ρn​‖wx−wy‖2+ρcn​∑i=1n‖Gi​x−Gi​y‖2\langle w_{x}-w_{y},x-y\rangle\geq-\rho_{n}\|w_{x}-w_{y}\|^{2}+\frac{\rho_{c}}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|G_{i}x-G_{i}y\|^{2}.

In particular, let us discuss the case when T=0T=0 and ρc>0\rho_{c}>0. Then, (6) reduces to

⟨G​x−G​y,x−y⟩≥−ρn​‖G​x−G​y‖2+ρc​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2],∀x,y∈dom⁡(G).{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle Gx-Gy,x-y\rangle\geq-\rho_{n}\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}+\rho_{c}\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big],\quad\forall x,y\in\mathrm{dom}(G).\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt (7)

We have the following facts corresponding to GG in this case.

  • •

    First, if 𝐆\mathbf{G} is deterministic, i.e., G​x≡𝐆⁡(x,ξ)Gx\equiv\mathbf{G}(x,\xi) in (1) or n=1n=1 in (2), then (7) reduces to ⟨G​x−G​y,x−y⟩≥−ρ​‖G​x−G​y‖2\langle Gx-Gy,x-y\rangle\geq-\rho\|Gx-Gy\|^{2} for ρ:=ρn−ρc\rho:=\rho_{n}-\rho_{c}. Clearly, if ρn<ρc\rho_{n}<\rho_{c}, then GG becomes |ρ||\rho|-co-coercive, a case excluded by Assumption 1 since we require ρn≥ρc\rho_{n}\geq\rho_{c}. If ρc=ρn\rho_{c}=\rho_{n}, then GG is monotone. If ρn>ρc\rho_{n}>\rho_{c}, then GG is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone (see Subsection 2.1 for the definition of these concepts).

  • •

    Second, since 𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]≥‖𝔼ξ​[𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)]‖2\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]\geq\|\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\big]\|^{2} by Jensen’s inequality, (7) implies that ⟨G​x−G​y,x−y⟩≥−ρ​‖G​x−G​y‖2\langle Gx-Gy,x-y\rangle\geq-\rho\|Gx-Gy\|^{2} for ρ:=ρn−ρc\rho:=\rho_{n}-\rho_{c}. Therefore, if ρn<ρc\rho_{n}<\rho_{c}, then (7) is slightly stronger than the |ρ||\rho|-co-coercivity of GG. If ρn>ρc\rho_{n}>\rho_{c}, then (7) is slightly stronger than the ρ\rho-co-hypomonotonicity of GG.

  • •

    Third, since ρn≥0\rho_{n}\geq 0, if ρc>0\rho_{c}>0, then (7) is considerably weaker than the ρc\rho_{c}-average co-coercivity of GG, i.e., ⟨G​x−G​y,x−y⟩≥ρc​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]\langle Gx-Gy,x-y\rangle\geq\rho_{c}\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]. This ρc\rho_{c}-average-co-coercivity assumption has been widely used in many recent works to develop variance reduction methods for (GE) and its special cases, see, e.g., [24, 33, 100, 102].

In this paper, we do not focus on the case ρn<ρc\rho_{n}<\rho_{c} in (7) because GG is (ρc−ρn)(\rho_{c}-\rho_{n})-co-coercive, which has been studied in previous works, including our papers [100, 102]. We only consider the case ρn≥ρc≥0\rho_{n}\geq\rho_{c}\geq 0, which covers a class of monotone and co-hypomonotone operators. Figure 1 illustrates the class of ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone operators GG as well as the class of GG satisfying condition (6) when ρc>0\rho_{c}>0. The latter intersects with both monotone and nonmonotone operators. Subsections 2.3 and 2.4 provide many examples of Φ\Phi and GG satisfying (6) and (7).

Note that if T=0T=0, then Assumption 1 implies the ρ\rho-co-hypomonotonicity of GG with ρ:=ρn−ρc\rho:=\rho_{n}-\rho_{c}. Thus, Assumption 1 automatically holds with ρ∗=ρ\rho_{*}=\rho. Alternatively, if ρc=0\rho_{c}=0, then Assumption 1 also implies the ρn\rho_{n}-co-hypomonotonicity of Φ\Phi, and hence, Assumption 1 also automatically holds with ρ∗=ρn\rho_{*}=\rho_{n}. In these two cases, Assumption 1 is redundant and can be removed.

1.2.\mathrm{1.2.} Motivation and challenges. Both minimax optimization and variational inequality (VIP) problems are fundamental and powerful tools for modeling two-person games, Nash equilibria, robust optimization [11, 23, 41, 89, 95, 94, 96], and more recently, generative adversarial learning, online learning, reinforcement learning, and distributionally robust optimization [6, 10, 14, 16, 43, 51, 66, 69, 71, 92, 107]. Their optimality conditions can be expressed as a generalized equation (GE). Yet, unlike classical models, modern applications are data-driven, large-scale, and often involve nonconvex, nonmonotone, and/or nonsmooth structures, limiting the use of deterministic and primal-dual approaches. Mathematically, these problems are typically formulated as large finite-sums or as stochastic expectations induced by sampled data. Consequently, contemporary methods face significant challenges, including restrictive assumptions, high computational operation cost, low efficiency, and slow convergence rates.

Hitherto, most methods developed for (GE) and its special cases are deterministic and primarily address monotone problems, see, e.g., [11, 41, 58]. They are inefficient for the finite-sum setting (2) when nn is large, and inapplicable to the expectation setting (1), where GG is not directly accessible. Randomized and stochastic methods exist for (GE), but under restrictive assumptions [21, 30, 31, 61, 87]. Many of these still rely on the classical Robbins-Monro approach without acceleration, resulting in slow convergence rates and oracle complexities often ranging from 𝒪⁡(ϵ−6)\mathcal{O}\big(\epsilon^{-6}\big) to 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4)\mathcal{O}\big(\epsilon^{-4}\big), depending on the method and assumptions, where ϵ\epsilon is a desired accuracy level.

Recently, several works have applied variance-reduction techniques using control variates, commonly developed in optimization, to (GE), improving oracle complexity over the classical stochastic approximation. However, these algorithms are non-accelerated with slow convergence rates, typically 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k\big), see, e.g., [1, 2, 33]. While [1, 2] rely on Lipschitz continuity of GG and monotonicity of Φ\Phi, others such as [24, 33, 100, 102] assume stronger conditions: co-coercivity and/or strong quasi-monotonicity. Co-coercivity is strong and hard to verify in practice; it is stronger than monotonicity plus Lipschitz continuity and fails for a bilinear mapping F​x=[𝐋​v,−𝐋T​u]Fx=[\mathbf{L}v,-\mathbf{L}^{T}u], where x=(u,v)x=(u,v) and 𝐋\mathbf{L} is given. Moreover, checking co-coercivity of the saddle mapping in minimax optimization applications is non-trivial, even in the convex-concave case.

1.3.\mathrm{1.3.} Our goal and approach. The above shortcomings raise the following research question: Can we develop a single-loop algorithmic framework capable of achieving faster 𝒪⁡(1/k2)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k^{2}\big) and o⁡(1/k2)o\big(1/k^{2}\big) convergence rates via acceleration, covering a wide range of variants ((using both unbiased and biased estimators)), attaining improved oracle complexity through variance reduction, and requiring weaker assumptions ((including a subclass of nonmonotone problems))?

This paper aims to address this question. However, we face two main technical challenges. First, classical Krasnosel’kiǐ-Mann (KM) iteration is not directly applicable under our assumptions, requiring a shift to extragradient-type (EG) schemes. Nevertheless, EG involves the composite mapping G⁡(x−η​G​x)G(x-\eta Gx), which complicates the design and analysis of stochastic algorithms. We instead exploit Popov’s past-extragradient method [90] (also closely related to the optimistic gradient scheme) to overcome this limitation. Second, developing variance-reduction methods with control variate techniques requires a structural assumption on GG, often called “average co-coercivity” [24, 33, 100, 102], which excludes certain problem classes, particularly nonmonotone ones. We identify a new class of problems that includes both monotone and nonmonotone operators. This class typically satisfies Assumptions 1, 1, and 1.

Unlike previous approaches, our algorithmic development simultaneously combines three main ideas: the past-extragradient method, Nesterov’s acceleration, and unbiased and biased variance-reduction techniques. While each has been studied extensively, their unified combination to solve (GE) under Assumptions 1-1 remains largely unexplored, especially for nonmonotone problems.

1.4.\mathrm{1.4.} Our contributions. To this end, our contributions consist of the following:

  • (a)\mathrm{(a)}

    First, we introduce Assumption 1 to identify a new class of problems in (GE) that goes beyond standard monotonicity and co-coercivity assumptions. Concrete examples in Subsection 2.4 illustrate the scope and relevance of this assumption, showing that it covers subclasses of both monotone and nonmonotone operators.

  • (b)\mathrm{(b)}

    Second, we develop a novel stochastic Nesterov-type accelerated past-extragradient framework to approximate solutions of (GE). Our framework only requires one stochastic approximation G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} of G​ykGy^{k} per iteration, evaluated at the iterate yky^{k}. We introduce a general error approximation condition connecting G​ykGy^{k} to its (unbiased or biased) stochastic variance-reduced estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k}, constructed via the stochastic oracle 𝐆⁡(⋅,ξ)\mathbf{G}(\cdot,\xi), which forms the basis of our convergence analysis. Alternatively, we also propose a class of control-variate-based estimators of GG for our framework, covering both unbiased and biased instances, including SVRG [54], SAGA [34], and SARAH [85].

  • (c)\mathrm{(c)}

    Third, we establish 𝒪⁡(1/k2)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k^{2}\big) convergence rates in expectation for 𝔼⁡[‖G​xk+vk‖2]\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}\big] using either the proposed error approximation criterion or our class of variance-reduced estimators, where xkx^{k} is the iterate and vk∈T​xkv^{k}\in Tx^{k}. Our rate is significantly better than non-accelerated counterparts, e.g., [1, 2, 101], by a factor of 1/k1/k. We further prove o⁡(1/k2)o\big(1/k^{2}\big) convergence of ‖G​xk+vk‖2\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2} both in expectation and almost surely, and show that the iterate sequences {xk}\{x^{k}\}, {yk}\{y^{k}\}, and {zk}\{z^{k}\} converge almost surely to a zer⁡(Φ)\mathrm{zer}(\Phi)-valued random variable x⋆x^{\star}, a solution of (GE).

  • (d)\mathrm{(d)}

    Finally, we demonstrate our framework with three common estimators: Loopless SVRG, SAGA, and Loopless SARAH, and analyze their oracle complexities for the finite-sum case (2). For Loopless SVRG and SAGA, we obtain 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡(n)+n2/3​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}\big(n\log(n)+n^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1}\big), while for Loopless SARAH we achieve 𝒪⁡(n​log⁡(n)+n1/2​ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}\big(n\log(n)+n^{1/2}\epsilon^{-1}\big), where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is the target accuracy.

We believe that our framework is simple to implement, as it is single-loop and uses elementary operations. Moreover, it includes a broad class of variance-reduced and accelerated algorithms, covering mini-batch, unbiased, and biased estimators, a feature that is rarely seen in optimization. Unlike most existing methods limited to the monotone setting or special cases of (GE), our approach can handle a class of nonmonotone generalized equations. Its convergence guarantees are notable, covering 𝒪⁡(1/k2)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k^{2}\big) and o⁡(1/k2)o\big(1/k^{2}\big) convergence rates, and almost sure convergence of iterates. The o⁡(1/k2)o\big(1/k^{2}\big) rates and almost-sure convergence of the iterates have received limited attention, even in variance-reduction methods for convex optimization.

1.5.\mathrm{1.5.} Related work and comparison. Problem (GE) is classical, with its theory and numerical methods extensively studied over decades, as presented in monographs such as [11, 41, 77, 95] and references therein. In this paper, we focus on a different class of (GE) and develop novel stochastic single-loop methods with acceleration and variance reduction. Accordingly, we restrict our review and comparison to works along this direction.

(a)\mathrm{(a)} From non-accelerated to accelerated methods. The key advantage of accelerated methods over non-accelerated ones is their faster convergence rates: 𝒪⁡(1/k2)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k^{2}\big) vs. 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k\big). Nesterov first introduced acceleration for smooth convex optimization [83], later extended to other problems and monotone inclusions, including (GE) [7, 9]. This line of research has recently gained strong attention, especially in deterministic settings [20, 22, 57, 72, 103, 104].

As an alternative, Halpern’s fixed-point iteration [49] also achieves accelerated 𝒪⁡(1/k2)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k^{2}\big) rates on the squared norm of residual for (GE) under co-coercivity [36, 68, 97], improving on the classical 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k\big) rate of the Krasnosel’kiǐ-Mann (KM) method and its variants.

These advances have driven extensive work in operator theory, mostly in deterministic settings [26, 27, 65, 103, 109]. Though Nesterov- and Halpern-type accelerations were developed independently, their connection was later established in [99] and also in [86]. In this paper, we build on Nesterov’s acceleration to design stochastic variance-reduction algorithms for (GE) under Assumptions 1–1 and establish their rigorous convergence guarantees.

(b)\mathrm{(b)} From convex optimization to generalized equations. In convex optimization, the LL-smoothness of the objective function is equivalent to its gradient co-coercivity [11, 84], making smooth convex minimization problems special cases of (NE) with GG being co-coercive. By contrast, smooth convex-concave minimax problems often lack this property (see, e.g., bilinear game models [41]), highlighting a key distinction between optimization and generalized equations (GE). This shift complicates algorithm design and convergence analysis, as many standard analysis tools in convex optimization no longer apply to (GE) [9, 57, 99]. One technical challenge is the absence of an objective function in (GE), complicating the construction of a suitable Lyapunov function that underpins convergence guarantees in accelerated methods. In addition, unlike optimization, developing accelerated randomized and variance-reduced methods for data-driven (GE) remains challenging but crucial.

Beyond co-coercivity, extragradient (EG) and its variants [59, 90, 32] are prominent, but their stochastic extensions face difficulties: dependence on intermediate updates [110] and the breakdown of gap function-based analysis under nonmonotonicity [1, 2]. Dual averaging and mirror descent [82, 61] are similarly restricted to monotone problems. In this work, we extend Popov’s past-extragradient variant to the stochastic setting, addressing cases with biased estimators.

(c)\mathrm{(c)} Comparison with existing stochastic methods. Stochastic methods for (GE) often follow the Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation framework, but converge slowly, typically at an 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k\big) rate with inefficient oracle complexity, see, e.g., [19, 28, 31, 52, 55, 56, 60]. Recent work improves this limitation via variance reduction techniques, e.g., adaptive or growing mini-batches [21, 87]. Alternative approaches such as dual averaging and mirror descent [29, 61] extend to VIPs but require monotonicity, limiting applicability. Other advances include stochastic splitting and mirror-prox methods [15, 44, 70]. In contrast, our work employs accelerated methods with a broad class of unbiased and biased variance-reduced estimators, including several well-known instances.

(d)\mathrm{(d)} Comparison with variance-reduction methods using control variate techniques. In the co-coercive setting, several variance-reduced methods using control variates have been proposed [24, 33, 100, 102], exploiting co-coercivity for faster rates and improved oracle complexity. Table 1 summarizes recent works by assumptions, estimators, and guarantees. Beyond co-coercivity, EG variants, often based on Popov’s scheme [90], have been studied for monotone VIPs. Examples include SVRG-based methods in [1, 2, 110], which use gap functions for convergence analysis and rely on bounded-variance or unbiased estimators.

Our approach retains a simple single-loop structure, similar to the methods in [1, 2, 24, 33], but it further (i) incorporates acceleration, (ii) applies to “co-hypomonotone-type” operators, (iii) accommodates both unbiased and biased estimators under general error-bound conditions, (iv) establishes stronger convergence guarantees, including o⁡(1/k2)o\big(1/k^{2}\big) rates in expectation and almost surely, as well as almost sure convergence of the iterates to a solution, and (v) achieves improved oracle complexity under weaker assumptions. Unlike [1, 110], our method also provides residual convergence guarantees with better oracle complexity in the finite-sum setting.

1.6.\mathrm{1.6.} Paper organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the necessary background and concepts, and presents examples of Φ\Phi and GG satisfying Assumption 1. Section 3 develops a unified accelerated past-extragradient-type framework with variance reduction to solve (GE) for the expectation setting (1) under Assumption 1, Assumption 1 with α=1\alpha=1, and Assumption 1 with ρc=0\rho_{c}=0, establishing convergence under a general error bound condition. Section 4 introduces an alternative variant using control-variate-based variance reduction to handle both (1) and (2), with similar convergence guarantees. Section 5 provides a complete convergence analysis of the proposed methods. Section 6 presents three numerical examples to validate our theoretical results and benchmark against state-of-the-art methods. Preliminary results and technical proofs are deferred to the appendix.

2 Background, Preliminaries, and Examples.

We recall necessary notation and concepts used in this paper, and briefly describe Popov’s method. Finally, we provide different examples to illustrate Assumption 1.

2.1 Notation and concepts.

First, we recall necessary notation and concepts.

Basic concepts. We work with a finite-dimensional space ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p} equipped with the standard inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle and norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. For a function f:ℝp→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}, ∇f\nabla{f} denotes the gradient of ff, ∂f\partial{f} denotes the subdifferential of ff, and proxf\mathrm{prox}_{f} is the proximal operator of ff. For a given random vector 𝐮ξ\mathbf{u}_{\xi} in ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p} and v∈ℝpv\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, we define u:=𝔼ξ​[𝐮ξ]u:=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\mathbf{u}_{\xi}] and |∥u+v|∥2:=𝔼ξ[∥𝐮ξ+v∥2]|\!\|u+v|\!\|^{2}:=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[\|\mathbf{u}_{\xi}+v\|^{2}]. By Jensen’s inequality, we also have |∥u+v|∥2≥∥u+v∥2|\!\|u+v|\!\|^{2}\geq\|u+v\|^{2}. For a given symmetric matrix 𝐐∈ℝp×p\mathbf{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}, 𝐐⪰0\mathbf{Q}\succeq 0 (resp., 𝐐≻0\mathbf{Q}\succ 0) means that 𝐐\mathbf{Q} is positive semidefinite (resp., positive definite). For two symmetric matrices 𝐏\mathbf{P} and 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, 𝐏⪰𝐐\mathbf{P}\succeq\mathbf{Q} means 𝐏−𝐐⪰0\mathbf{P}-\mathbf{Q}\succeq 0. For given functions g⁡(t)g(t) and h⁡(t)h(t), we say that g⁡(t)=𝒪⁡(h⁡(t))g(t)=\mathcal{O}\big(h(t)\big) if there exist M>0M>0 and t0≥0t_{0}\geq 0 such that g⁡(t)≤M​h​(t)g(t)\leq Mh(t) for t≥t0t\geq t_{0}. We use 𝒪~​(g​(t))\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(g(t)) to hide a poly-log factor of g⁡(t)g(t).

Filtration and expectations. Let ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} denote the σ\sigma-algebra generated by all the randomness of our algorithm up to iteration kk, including the iterates x0,⋯,xkx^{0},\cdots,x^{k}. We also denote by 𝔼k[⋅]:=𝔼[⋅∣ℱk]\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\cdot\big]:=\mathbb{E}\big[\cdot\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}\big] the conditional expectation conditioned on ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}, and by 𝔼⁡[⋅]\mathbb{E}\big[\cdot\big] the full expectation. For a random variable ξ\xi, we denote by 𝔼ξ​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\cdot\big] the expectation w.r.t. ξ\xi.

Lipschitz continuity. For a single-valued mapping G:ℝp→ℝpG:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}, we say that GG is LL-Lipschitz continuous if there exists L≥0L\geq 0 such that ‖G​x−G​y‖≤L​‖x−y‖\|Gx-Gy\|\leq L\|x-y\| for all x,y∈dom⁡(G)x,y\in\mathrm{dom}(G). If L<1L<1, then GG is contractive, and if L=1L=1, then GG is nonexpansive.

Co-monotonicity, monotonicity, and co-coercivity. For a single-valued or multivalued mapping G:ℝp⇉ℝpG:\mathbb{R}^{p}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^{p}, we denote by dom⁡(G):={x∈ℝp:G​x≠∅}\mathrm{dom}(G):=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:Gx\neq\emptyset\} the domain of GG and by gra⁡(G):={(x,u)∈ℝp×ℝp:u∈G​x}\mathrm{gra}(G):=\{(x,u)\in\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{p}:u\in Gx\} the graph of GG. If GG is differentiable at xx, then G′​(x)G^{\prime}(x) denotes its derivative at xx. We say that GG has a closed graph gra⁡(G)\mathrm{gra}(G) if for any sequence {(xk,uk)}\{(x^{k},u^{k})\} such that (xk,uk)∈gra⁡(G)(x^{k},u^{k})\in\mathrm{gra}(G) and (xk,uk)→(x,u)(x^{k},u^{k})\to(x,u) as k→∞k\to\infty, then (x,u)∈gra⁡(G)(x,u)\in\mathrm{gra}(G). For further details on these concepts and properties, we refer the reader to [11].

Definition 2.1

Let G:ℝp→2ℝpG:\mathbb{R}^{p}\to 2^{\mathbb{R}^{p}} be a given single-valued or multivalued mapping.

  • •

    We say that GG is monotone if for all (x,u),(y,v)∈gra⁡(G)(x,u),(y,v)\in\mathrm{gra}(G), we have ⟨u−v,x−y⟩≥0\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq 0.

  • •

    We say that GG is ρ\rho-co-monotone if there exists ρ∈ℝ\rho\in\mathbb{R} such that ⟨u−v,x−y⟩≥ρ​‖u−v‖2\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq\rho\|u-v\|^{2} for all (x,u),(y,v)∈gra⁡(G)(x,u),(y,v)\in\mathrm{gra}(G). Clearly, if ρ=0\rho=0, then GG reduces to a monotone mapping. See [12] for the definitions and further properties.

    • ⋄\diamond

      If ⟨u−v,x−y⟩≥ρ​‖u−v‖2\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq\rho\|u-v\|^{2} for ρ<0\rho<0, then we say that GG is |ρ||\rho|-co-hypomonotone. A |ρ||\rho|-co-hypomonotone mapping can be nonmonotone (see examples, e.g., in [102]).

    • ⋄\diamond

      If ⟨u−v,x−y⟩≥ρ​‖u−v‖2\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq\rho\|u-v\|^{2} for ρ>0\rho>0, then we say that GG is ρ\rho-co-coercive. Moreover, if GG is ρ\rho-co-coercive, then it is also monotone and LL-Lipschitz continuous with L:=1ρL:=\frac{1}{\rho}.

If ff is a convex and LL-smooth (i.e., ∇f\nabla{f} is LL-Lipschitz continuous) function, then ∇f\nabla{f} is 1L\frac{1}{L}-co-coercive. The ρ\rho-co-coercivity of a mapping GG is also equivalent to the nonexpansiveness of F=𝕀−2​ρ​GF=\mathbb{I}-2\rho G in the fixed-point problem (FP), see [11]. All the concepts defined above are global. If GG satisfies any of the above properties for all (x,u),(y,v)∈gra⁡(G)∩𝒲(x,u),(y,v)\in\mathrm{gra}(G)\cap\mathcal{W}, where 𝒲\mathcal{W} is a neighborhood of (x¯,u¯)(\bar{x},\bar{u}) in ℝp×ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{p}, then we say that GG has such a local property around (x¯,u¯)∈gra⁡(G)(\bar{x},\bar{u})\in\mathrm{gra}(G).

2.2 The past-extragradient method.

A classical method for solving (GE) in the variational inequality setting T=𝒩𝒳T=\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{X}} (the normal cone of 𝒳\mathcal{X}), where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is nonempty, closed, and convex and GG is monotone and Lipschitz continuous, is Korpelevich’s extragradient method, introduced by Korpelevich in [59] in 1976 (also by Antipin in [4] (1976)). This method has inspired various variants, among which the past-extragradient method, a notable variant proposed by Popov in [90], is particularly well-known. When applied to solving (GE), this variant is equivalent to the optimistic gradient method studied in [32, 76, 79].

This method starts from x0∈dom⁡(Φ)x^{0}\in\mathrm{dom}(\Phi), chooses y−1:=x0y^{-1}:=x^{0}, and at each iteration k≥0k\geq 0, updates

{yk:⁣=Jη​T​(xk−η​G​yk−1),xk+1:⁣=Jη​T​(xk−η​G​yk),\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}y^{k}&:=&J_{\eta T}(x^{k}-\eta Gy^{k-1}),\\ x^{k+1}&:=&J_{\eta T}(x^{k}-\eta Gy^{k}),\end{array}\right. (PEG)

where η>0\eta>0 is a given stepsize. This scheme has been well studied in the literature, including [75, 90, 105], mostly in the deterministic setting. It also has close connections to other methods such as the projected reflected gradient scheme [73], the forward-reflected-backward splitting algorithm [75], and the golden-ratio method [74]. As mentioned, when T=0T=0, it is also equivalent to the optimistic gradient method [32, 76, 79]. Inspired by (PEG), we develop an accelerated algorithmic framework with variance reduction in Section 3 to solve (GE) under Assumptions 1-1.

2.3 Examples of co-hypomonotone operators.

We provide here a number of mappings that are co-hypomonotone, but not necessarily monotone.

(a)\mathrm{(a)} Example 1. As shown in [102], given a p×pp\times p symmetric and invertible matrix 𝐆\mathbf{G} and a vector 𝐠∈ℝp\mathbf{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, an affine mapping G​x:=𝐆​x+𝐠Gx:=\mathbf{G}x+\mathbf{g} is ρ\rho-co-monotone with ρ:=λmin​(𝐆−1)\rho:=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{G}^{-1}). If ρ:=λmin​(𝐆−1)<0\rho:=\lambda_{\min}(\mathbf{G}^{-1})<0, then GG is nonmonotone, but |ρ||\rho|-co-hypomonotone. More generally, for an arbitrary matrix 𝐆∈ℝp×p\mathbf{G}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}, the affine mapping G​x:=𝐆​x+𝐠Gx:=\mathbf{G}x+\mathbf{g} is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone for some ρ≥0\rho\geq 0 if and only if 𝐆+𝐆⊤+2​ρ​𝐆⊤​𝐆⪰0\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\top}+2\rho\mathbf{G}^{\top}\mathbf{G}\succeq 0. As shown in Example 4 below, the subdifferentials of certain nonconvex regularizers are not linear but piecewise linear, and they are also locally ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone.

(b)\mathrm{(b)} Example 2. As shown in [40, Proposition 4.17], consider a twice continuously differentiable function Ψ:ℝp1×ℝp2→ℝ\Psi:\mathbb{R}^{p_{1}}\times\mathbb{R}^{p_{2}}\to\mathbb{R} and its associated saddle mapping Φ⁡(u,v):=[∇uΨ​(u,v),−∇vΨ​(u,v)]\Phi(u,v):=[\nabla_{u}\Psi(u,v),-\nabla_{v}\Psi(u,v)]. If Ψ\Psi satisfies the α\alpha-interaction-dominance condition with α≥0\alpha\geq 0 and parameter ρ>0\rho>0, then Φ\Phi is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone. The interaction-dominance condition was introduced in [48] for studying smooth nonconvex-nonconcave minimax problems. Recently, [40] generalized co-hypomonotonicity to semi-monotonicity, which encompasses both hypomonotonicity and co-hypomonotonicity while covering broader parameter regimes.

(c)\mathrm{(c)} Example 3. Let A:ℝp⇉ℝpA:\mathbb{R}^{p}\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^{p} be a monotone operator and ρ>0\rho>0 be given. Then, the mapping T​x:=−ρ−1​x−A​xTx:=-\rho^{-1}x-Ax is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone and, in general, nonmonotone (see Appendix A.2).

(d)\mathrm{(d)} Example 4. As shown in [102], consider the [generalized] subdifferential T​x:=∂SCADa​(x)Tx:=\partial{\mathrm{SCAD}_{a}}(x) of the SCAD (smoothly clipped absolute deviation) regularizer from [42] with a=3.7a=3.7, which is widely used in statistics. The operator TT is not globally ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone. However, on each smooth concave region of SCADa\mathrm{SCAD}_{a}, it is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone, where ρ:=a−1\rho:=a-1. More precisely, ⟨u−v,x−y⟩=−(a−1)​‖u−v‖2\langle u-v,x-y\rangle=-(a-1)\|u-v\|^{2} for all (x,u),(y,v)∈gra⁡(T)(x,u),(y,v)\in\mathrm{gra}(T) belonging to the same concave region. Similar local co-hypomonotonicity properties hold for several other well-known nonconvex regularizers, such as MCP (minimax concave penalty) and the log-sum penalty.

3 Variance Reduced Fast Optimistic Gradient Method for the General Case.

In this section, we exploit three main ideas: Popov’s past-EG scheme, Nesterov’s acceleration, and variance reduction techniques to develop a novel algorithmic framework for solving a class of (GE) under the Lipschitz continuity of GG and the ρn\rho_{n}-co-hypomonotonicity of Φ\Phi. That is: we solve a class of (GE) covered by Assumption 1 with α=1\alpha=1 and Assumption 1 with ρn≥0\rho_{n}\geq 0 and ρc=0\rho_{c}=0.

3.1 The proposed algorithm.

The following variant of Nesterov’s accelerated method from [13, 83] for minimizing the sum ϕ:=f+g\phi:=f+g of a convex and LL-smooth function ff and a possibly nonsmooth and convex function gg can be expressed as follows:

{x^k:⁣=tk−stk​xk+stk​zk,xk+1:⁣=x^k−η⁡(∇f​(x^k)+vk+1),zk+1:⁣=zk−η​tks​(∇f​(x^k)+vk+1),\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\hat{x}^{k}&:=&\frac{t_{k}-s}{t_{k}}x^{k}+\frac{s}{t_{k}}z^{k},\\ x^{k+1}&:=&\hat{x}^{k}-\eta(\nabla{f}(\hat{x}^{k})+v^{k+1}),\\ z^{k+1}&:=&z^{k}-\frac{\eta t_{k}}{s}(\nabla{f}(\hat{x}^{k})+v^{k+1}),\end{array}\right.\vskip-2.15277pt (NAG)

where vk+1∈∂g⁡(xk+1)v^{k+1}\in\partial{g}(x^{k+1}), 0<η≤1L0<\eta\leq\frac{1}{L} is a given stepsize, and tk=k+s+1t_{k}=k+s+1 for some s>1s>1. Here, we have used the identity xk+1=proxη​g​(xk+1+η​vk+1)x^{k+1}=\mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}(x^{k+1}+\eta v^{k+1}) in the second line. This algorithm is known to achieve an 𝒪⁡(1/k2)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k^{2}\big) convergence rate on the objective residual ϕ⁡(xk)−ϕ⁡(x⋆)\phi(x^{k})-\phi(x^{\star}), significantly improving over the 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k\big) rate in the standard proximal gradient method. Under an appropriate choice of ss, (NAG) can achieve up to an o⁡(1/k2)o\big(1/k^{2}\big) rate [8].

Main idea. Our idea is to exploit this (NAG) scheme and combine it with Popov’s past-EG mechanism to develop an accelerated past-extragradient scheme for (GE). However, since we can only access an unbiased stochastic oracle 𝐆\mathbf{G} of GG, we will approximate the value G​ykGy^{k} by a stochastic variance-reduced estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} constructed from 𝐆⁡(yk,ξ)\mathbf{G}(y^{k},\xi). This combination leads to the following new Variance-reduced Accelerated Past ExtraGradient method, which we call VAPEG.

The proposed method. Given an initial point x0∈ℝpx^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}, we set z0=y−1:=x0z^{0}=y^{-1}:=x^{0}, G~​y−1=G~​y−1:=G~​x0\widetilde{G}y^{-1}=\widetilde{G}y^{-1}:=\widetilde{G}x^{0}, and at each iteration k≥0k\geq 0, we construct a stochastic estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} of G​ykGy^{k}, and then update

{x^k:⁣=tk−stk​xk+stk​zk,yk:⁣=x^k−(η−βk)​(G~​yk−1+vk),xk+1:⁣=x^k−η⁡(G~​yk+vk+1)+βk​(G~​yk−1+vk),zk+1:⁣=zk−γks​(G~​yk−1+vk),\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\hat{x}^{k}&:=&\frac{t_{k}-s}{t_{k}}x^{k}+\frac{s}{t_{k}}z^{k},\\ y^{k}&:=&\hat{x}^{k}-(\eta-\beta_{k})(\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}+v^{k}),\\ x^{k+1}&:=&\hat{x}^{k}-\eta(\widetilde{G}y^{k}+v^{k+1})+\beta_{k}(\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}+v^{k}),\\ z^{k+1}&:=&z^{k}-\frac{\gamma_{k}}{s}(\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}+v^{k}),\end{array}\right. (VAPEG)

where vk∈T​xkv^{k}\in Tx^{k}, tk≥s>1t_{k}\geq s>1, η>0\eta>0, βk≥0\beta_{k}\geq 0, γk>0\gamma_{k}>0 are given parameters, determined later. There are two key components of (VAPEG) that require further discussion.

  • •

    First, we will clearly characterize the conditions on the estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} of G​ykGy^{k} to guarantee the convergence of (VAPEG). We will also give concrete examples of G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k}.

  • •

    Second, we will specify the choice of parameters tkt_{k}, ss, η\eta, βk\beta_{k}, and γk\gamma_{k} in our convergence analysis to achieve better convergence than its non-accelerated counterparts.

The scheme (VAPEG) is sufficiently general to cover the following special cases.

  • (a)\mathrm{(a)}

    If G~​yk:=G​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k}:=Gy^{k} and G~​yk−1:=G​xk\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}:=Gx^{k}, then we obtain a deterministic fast extragradient method for solving (GE). It is similar to the one in [104, 111], but the last step is different.

  • (b)\mathrm{(b)}

    If G~​yk:=G​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k}:=Gy^{k} and G~​yk−1:=G​yk−1\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}:=Gy^{k-1}, then we get a deterministic accelerated past-extragradient or fast optimistic gradient (OG) method for solving (GE). This deterministic variant is also new under Assumptions 1-1, and also different from [104].

Comparison with (PEG) and (NAG). In fact, (VAPEG) mimics Popov’s past-extragradient scheme, Nesterov’s acceleration, and variance reduction techniques to create such a new algorithm. Formally, if T=0T=0, G~​yk=G​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k}=Gy^{k}, βk=0\beta_{k}=0, and s=0s=0, then this scheme reduces to (PEG) discussed in Section 2. At the same time, it incorporates an intermediate step x^k=tk−stk​xk+stk​zk\hat{x}^{k}=\frac{t_{k}-s}{t_{k}}x^{k}+\frac{s}{t_{k}}z^{k} and uses the varying parameters tkt_{k} and βk\beta_{k}, similarly to Nesterov’s accelerated method (NAG) in convex optimization. However, the first fundamental difference between (NAG) and (VAPEG) is the use of the stepsize γks\frac{\gamma_{k}}{s} instead of η​tks\frac{\eta t_{k}}{s} in the last line of (VAPEG). The second one is the search direction η​G~​yk−βk​G~​yk−1\eta\widetilde{G}y^{k}-\beta_{k}\widetilde{G}y^{k-1} in (VAPEG) combining two consecutive approximations G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} and G~​yk−1\widetilde{G}y^{k-1} of GG, which acts like η∇f(x^k)\eta\nabla{f}(\hat{x}^{k}) in (NAG) for smooth and convex optimization.

The implementable version. Since vk+1v^{k+1} is on the right-hand side of the third line of (VAPEG), we can use the resolvent Jη​TJ_{\eta T} of η​T\eta T to rewrite it equivalently to

{x^k:⁣=stk​zk+tk−stk​xk,yk:⁣=x^k−(η−βk)​(G~​yk−1+vk),xk+1:⁣=Jη​T​(x^k−η​G~​yk+βk​(G~​yk−1+vk)),zk+1:⁣=zk−γks​(G~​yk−1+vk),vk+1:⁣=1η​(x^k−xk+1+βk​(G~​yk−1+vk))−G~​yk.\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\hat{x}^{k}&:=&\frac{s}{t_{k}}z^{k}+\frac{t_{k}-s}{t_{k}}x^{k},\\ y^{k}&:=&\hat{x}^{k}-(\eta-\beta_{k})(\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}+v^{k}),\\ x^{k+1}&:=&J_{\eta T}\big(\hat{x}^{k}-\eta\widetilde{G}y^{k}+\beta_{k}(\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}+v^{k})\big),\\ z^{k+1}&:=&z^{k}-\frac{\gamma_{k}}{s}(\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}+v^{k}),\\ v^{k+1}&:=&\frac{1}{\eta}\big(\hat{x}^{k}-x^{k+1}+\beta_{k}(\widetilde{G}y^{k-1}+v^{k})\big)-\widetilde{G}y^{k}.\end{array}\right. (14)

Clearly, each iteration of (14) requires one construction of the estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} and one evaluation of Jη​TJ_{\eta T}. Note that, for our theoretical analysis, we require the exact evaluation of the resolvent Jη​TJ_{\eta T}. This requirement is satisfied in many cases where TT has a “simple form,” such as the subdifferential of a proximally tractable function (e.g., ∥⋅∥1\|\cdot\|_{1}, coordinate-wise separable functions, or the indicator function of a simple convex set). In practice, however, the resolvent Jη​TJ_{\eta T} can also be evaluated approximately to a prescribed accuracy, thereby broadening the applicability of our method (14), see, e.g., [94].

3.2 Main result 1: Convergence properties of VAPEG.

There are different strategies to approximate G​ykGy^{k} by G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k}. For instance, one can use increasing mini-batch stochastic approximation strategies as in [21, 87] or control variate techniques as in [34, 54, 85]. In what follows, we do not specify how to approximate G​ykGy^{k}, but introduce a general recursive bound for 𝔼k​[‖G~​yk−G​yk‖2]\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|\widetilde{G}y^{k}-Gy^{k}\|^{2}\big].

3.2.1 Error approximation condition between G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} and G​ykGy^{k}.

We assume that G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} is constructed by accessing the unbiased stochastic oracle 𝐆⁡(yk,ξ)\mathbf{G}(y^{k},\xi) of G​ykGy^{k} adapted to the filtration {ℱk}\{\mathcal{F}_{k}\} such that for k≥0k\geq 0, there exist two constants κ∈(0,1]\kappa\in(0,1] and Θ≥0\Theta\geq 0, a nonnegative sequence {δk}\{\delta_{k}\}, and a sequence of nonnegative random variables {Δk}\{\Delta_{k}\} such that the following condition holds almost surely for the error term ek:=G~​yk−G​yke^{k}:=\widetilde{G}y^{k}-Gy^{k}:

{𝔼k​[‖ek‖2]≤𝔼k​[Δk],𝔼k​[Δk]≤(1−κ)​Δk−1+Θ​L2​‖xk−yk−1‖2+δktk2,{\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]&\leq&\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\Delta_{k}\big],\\ \mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\Delta_{k}\big]&\leq&(1-\kappa)\Delta_{k-1}+\Theta L^{2}\|x^{k}-y^{k-1}\|^{2}+\frac{\delta_{k}}{t_{k}^{2}},\end{array}\right.}\vskip-2.15277pt (15)

where {(xk,yk)}\{(x^{k},y^{k})\} and {tk}\{t_{k}\} are updated by our scheme (VAPEG).

The condition (15) is rather general. Indeed, if κ=1\kappa=1 and Θ=0\Theta=0, then it reduces to 𝔼k​[‖ek‖2]≤δktk2\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\delta_{k}}{t_{k}^{2}}. If κ=1\kappa=1 and δk=0\delta_{k}=0, then it becomes 𝔼k​[‖ek‖2]≤Θ​L2​‖xk−yk−1‖2\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\Theta L^{2}\|x^{k}-y^{k-1}\|^{2}, which can be viewed as an adaptive error bound condition. One way to choose δk\delta_{k} is δk:=δ(k+r+1)1+ν\delta_{k}:=\frac{\delta}{(k+r+1)^{1+\nu}} for any ν≥0\nu\geq 0 and given δ≥0\delta\geq 0 and r>2r>2. In the sequel, we will denote by 𝒮K:=∑k=0Kδk\mathcal{S}_{K}:=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\delta_{k} and 𝒮∞:=∑k=0∞δk\mathcal{S}_{\infty}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_{k}.

Adaptive mini-batch estimator. One way to construct G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} is to use a mini-batch estimator with adaptively increasing size. Given a mini-batch ℬk\mathcal{B}_{k} of size bkb_{k}, we construct

G~​yk:⁣=1bk​∑ξk∈ℬk𝐆⁡(yk,ξk).{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\widetilde{G}y^{k}&:=&\frac{1}{b_{k}}\sum_{\xi_{k}\in\mathcal{B}_{k}}\mathbf{G}(y^{k},\xi_{k}).\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt (16)

It is well-known that 𝔼ℬk​[‖G~​yk−G​yk‖2]≤σ2bk\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}\big[\|\widetilde{G}y^{k}-Gy^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b_{k}}, where σ2\sigma^{2} is the variance of the stochastic oracle 𝐆\mathbf{G} in Assumption 1. To guarantee the condition (15), we need to choose bkb_{k} adaptively. For example, we can choose bkb_{k} using the following condition:

σ2bk≤(1−κ)​σ2bk−1+Θ​L2​‖xk−yk−1‖2+δktk2.{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b_{k}}\leq\frac{(1-\kappa)\sigma^{2}}{b_{k-1}}+\Theta L^{2}\|x^{k}-y^{k-1}\|^{2}+\frac{\delta_{k}}{t_{k}^{2}}.\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt (17)

Clearly, by setting Δk:=σ2bk\Delta_{k}:=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b_{k}}, G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} defined by (16) satisfies (15). Moreover, the condition (17) can be guaranteed by choosing an appropriate increasing mini-batch size bkb_{k}. This technique has been used in several previous works such as [21, 87]. Nevertheless, (15) can cover a wide range of estimators, including unbiased and biased instances, beyond the classical mini-batch instance (16).

This is also the number of evaluations of Jη​TJ_{\eta T}.

3.2.3 Almost sure convergence.

Next, we state the almost sure convergence rates and the almost sure convergence of iterates in the following theorem, whose proof is given in Subsection 5.2.

Theorem 3.2

Under the same assumptions and settings as in Theorem 3.1, assuming that 𝒮∞:=∑k=0∞δk<+∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_{k}<+\infty, we have the following statements.

  • (a)\mathrm{(a)}

    The following summability results hold:

    ∑k=0∞(k+1)​‖G​xk+vk‖2<+∞,almost surely,∑k=0∞(k+s)​‖G​yk−1+vk‖2<+∞,almost surely.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}&<&+\infty,\quad\textrm{almost surely},\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+s)\|Gy^{k-1}+v^{k}\|^{2}&<&+\infty,\quad\textrm{almost surely}.\end{array} (24)
  • (b)\mathrm{(b)}

    The following limits hold almost surely:

    limk→∞k2​‖G​xk+vk‖2=0andlimk→∞k2​‖G​yk−1+vk‖2=0.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\lim_{k\to\infty}k^{2}\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}=0\quad\textrm{and}\quad\lim_{k\to\infty}k^{2}\|Gy^{k-1}+v^{k}\|^{2}=0.\end{array} (25)
  • (c)\mathrm{(c)}

    If, additionally, gra⁡(Φ)\mathrm{gra}(\Phi) is closed, then {xk}\{x^{k}\} almost surely converges to a zer⁡(Φ)\mathrm{zer}(\Phi)-valued random variable x⋆∈zer⁡(Φ)x^{\star}\in\mathrm{zer}(\Phi). In addition, the other two sequences of iterates {yk}\{y^{k}\} and {zk}\{z^{k}\} also almost surely converge to the same random variable x⋆∈zer⁡(Φ)x^{\star}\in\mathrm{zer}(\Phi).

Note that if Assumption 1 holds with ρc=0\rho_{c}=0, then Assumption 1 also automatically holds with ρ∗=ρn\rho_{*}=\rho_{n}. Therefore, we do not require Assumption 1 in Theorems 3.1 and 3.2.

If TT is ρT\rho_{T}-co-hypomonotone for some ρT≥0\rho_{T}\geq 0, then, as proven in [102], the resolvent Jλ​TJ_{\lambda T} is well-defined, single-valued, and nonexpansive if λ>ρT\lambda>\rho_{T}. Let us define the following forward-backward splitting (FBS) residual of (GE), widely used in monotone operator theory:

𝒢λ​x:=1λ​(x−Jλ​T​(x−λ​G​x)).\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}x:=\frac{1}{\lambda}\big(x-J_{\lambda T}(x-\lambda Gx)\big).\end{array} (26)

It is well-known that x⋆∈zer⁡(Φ)x^{\star}\in\mathrm{zer}(\Phi) iff 𝒢λ​x⋆=0\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}x^{\star}=0. Therefore, for a given tolerance ϵ>0\epsilon>0, we can say that xkx^{k} is an ϵ\epsilon-solution of (GE) (in expectation) if 𝔼⁡[‖𝒢λ​xk‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}x^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2}. Since ‖𝒢λ​xk‖≤‖G​xk+vk‖\|\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}x^{k}\|\leq\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\| for any vk∈T​xkv^{k}\in Tx^{k} (see [105]), if we obtain 𝔼⁡[‖G​xk+vk‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2} as in Theorem 3.1, then we conclude that xkx^{k} is also an ϵ\epsilon-solution of (GE), i.e., 𝔼⁡[‖𝒢λ​xk‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}x^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2}.

Remark 3.3

Note that if Φ\Phi is maximally monotone, then gra⁡(Φ)\mathrm{gra}(\Phi) is closed, see [11, Proposition 20.38]. The closed-graph assumption is weaker than maximal monotonicity and is satisfied by many classes of continuous or closed set-valued mappings. In the single-valued case, one can replace this closedness assumption of gra⁡(Φ)\mathrm{gra}(\Phi) by a demiclosedness of Φ\Phi, see, e.g., [33]. If T=0T=0, then Φ=G\Phi=G, which is continuous, and thus gra⁡(G)\mathrm{gra}(G) is closed.

3.3 Oracle complexity of VAPEG with adaptive mini-batching estimators.

Now, we estimate the oracle complexity of (VAPEG) using the adaptive mini-batch estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} in (16) in the following corollary, whose proof can be found in Appendix C.5.

Corollary 3.4

Under the same conditions and settings as in Theorem 3.1, if G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} constructed by (16) with increasing mini-batch size bk:=⌈σ2​(k+s+1)3+νδ⌉b_{k}:=\big\lceil\frac{\sigma^{2}(k+s+1)^{3+\nu}}{\delta}\big\rceil for some constants ν>0\nu>0 and δ>0\delta>0 is used in (VAPEG), then the expected total number of oracle calls 𝐆\mathbf{G} to achieve xKx^{K} such that 𝔼⁡[‖G​xK+vK‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{K}+v^{K}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2} for a given tolerance ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and vK∈T​xKv^{K}\in Tx^{K} is at most 𝔼⁡[𝒯K]=𝒪⁡(σ2ϵ4+ν)\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{4+\nu}}\big). The expected total number of Jη​TJ_{\eta T} evaluations is at most 𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)\mathcal{O}\big(\epsilon^{-1}\big).

Alternatively, if we choose bk:=⌈σ2​(k+s+1)3​log⁡(k+s+1)δ⌉b_{k}:=\big\lceil\frac{\sigma^{2}(k+s+1)^{3}\log(k+s+1)}{\delta}\big\rceil, then the above complexity is improved to 𝔼​[𝒯K]=𝒪~​(σ2ϵ4)\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]=\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{4}}\big). In this case, the expected total number of Jη​TJ_{\eta T} evaluations is at most 𝒪~​(ϵ−1)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1}).

The work [21] studied VIPs, a special case of (GE), and established a 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4​ln⁡(ϵ−1))\mathcal{O}\big(\epsilon^{-4}\ln(\epsilon^{-1})\big) oracle complexity using increasing mini-batch estimators as (16). Our complexity in Corollary 3.4 is either 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4+ν)\mathcal{O}\big(\epsilon^{-4+\nu}\big) for any sufficiently small ν>0\nu>0 or 𝒪⁡(ϵ−4​ln⁡(ln⁡(ϵ−1)))\mathcal{O}\big(\epsilon^{-4}\ln(\ln(\epsilon^{-1}))\big) depending on the choice of bkb_{k}, which is comparable with [21]. Nevertheless, our assumptions, Assumptions 1 and 1, are different from the pseudo-monotonicity in [21]. Moreover, as mentioned earlier, our method can work with any unbiased and biased estimators under the condition (15), beyond (16). Increasing mini-batches were also used in [87], but the authors did not explicitly derive any oracle complexity, and also used different assumptions and metrics.

Note that our mini-batch size bkb_{k} in Corollary 3.4 is loosely chosen from the condition (15) with κ=1\kappa=1 and Θ=0\Theta=0. However, we can directly use the condition (17) to estimate bkb_{k}, which gives us a smaller batch size than the worst case bkb_{k} chosen in Corollary 3.4.

Corollary 3.4 also shows that if we use standard stochastic approximation (16) for G​ykGy^{k}, then our accelerated method (VAPEG) does not achieve better complexity than 𝒪~​(ϵ−4)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-4}). This is due to the accumulation of errors in accelerated methods compared to non-accelerated ones as studied in [35]. To achieve better complexity bounds, other variance-reduction techniques should be exploited. For example, in Section 4 below, we will use control variate techniques.

4 Convergence and Complexity of VAPEG using Control Variate Estimators.

In this section, we will employ control variate techniques to develop a variance-reduction variant of (VAPEG). Unlike Section 3, we let α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1) in Assumption 1 and require ρc>0\rho_{c}>0 in Assumption 1.

4.1 A class of stochastic variance-reduced estimators.

We propose to use the following class of variance-reduced estimators G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} of G​ykGy^{k}, which was introduced in our recent work [102]. This class of estimators is relatively broad and covers various well-known instances, including Loopless SVRG, SAGA, and Loopless SARAH.

Definition 4.1

Given κ¯∈(0,1)\underline{\kappa}\in(0,1) and Θ>0\Theta>0, let {yk}\{y^{k}\} be the sequence of iterates generated by (VAPEG) and G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} be a stochastic estimator of G​ykGy^{k} constructed from an i.i.d. sample ℬk⊆[n]\mathcal{B}_{k}\subseteq[n], adapted to the filtration {ℱk}\{\mathcal{F}_{k}\}. We say that G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} satisfies a VR​(Δk,κk,Θk,δk)\textbf{VR}(\Delta_{k};\kappa_{k},\Theta_{k},\delta_{k}) ((variance-reduction)) property if there exist two parameters κk∈[κ¯,1]\kappa_{k}\in[\underline{\kappa},1] and Θk∈[Θ¯,Θ¯]\Theta_{k}\in[\underline{\Theta},\bar{\Theta}], a nonnegative sequence {δk}\left\{\delta_{k}\right\}, and a nonnegative random quantity Δk\Delta_{k} such that ((almost surely)):

{𝔼k​[‖G~​yk−G​yk‖2]≤𝔼k​[Δk],𝔼k​[Δk]≤(1−κk)​Δk−1+Θk​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(yk,ξ)−𝐆⁡(yk−1,ξ)‖2]+δktk2,{\left\{\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|\widetilde{G}y^{k}-Gy^{k}\|^{2}\big]&\leq&\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\Delta_{k}\big],\\ \mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\Delta_{k}\big]&\leq&(1-\kappa_{k})\Delta_{k-1}+\Theta_{k}\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(y^{k},\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y^{k-1},\xi)\|^{2}\big]+\frac{\delta_{k}}{t_{k}^{2}},\end{array}\right.}\vskip-2.15277pt (27)

where {yk}\{y^{k}\} and {tk}\{t_{k}\} are updated by our scheme (VAPEG).

Definition 4.1 covers both unbiased and biased estimators G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} of G​ykGy^{k} since we do not impose the unbiased condition 𝔼ℬk​[G~​yk]=G​yk\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}\big[\widetilde{G}y^{k}\big]=Gy^{k}. It is also different from existing works, including [38, 100, 101], as we only require the condition (27), making it broader and allowing it to cover several existing estimators that may violate the definitions in [38, 100, 101]. Our class is also different from other generalizations such as [15, 44, 70] for stochastic optimization since they required the unbiasedness and additional or different conditions.

Now we provide three examples: Loopless SVRG, SAGA, and Loopless SARAH, that satisfy Definition 4.1. Note that the Loopless SVRG and SAGA are unbiased, whereas the Loopless SARAH is biased. In this paper, we only focus on these three estimators, but we believe that other variance-reduced estimators such as Hybrid SGD [106], SAG [64, 98], SARGE [39], SEGA [50], and JacSketch [46] could also be used in our methods.

4.1.1 Example 1: L-SVRG estimator.

SVRG was introduced in [54], and its Loopless version, called L-SVRG, was proposed in [62]. We show that this estimator satisfies Definition 4.1.

For given GG in (GE), two iterates yky^{k} and y¯k\bar{y}^{k}, and i.i.d. sample ℬk\mathcal{B}_{k} of size bkb_{k}, we define 𝐆ℬk​(⋅):=1bk​∑ξk∈ℬk𝐆⁡(⋅,ξk)\mathbf{G}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}(\cdot):=\frac{1}{b_{k}}\sum_{\xi_{k}\in\mathcal{B}_{k}}\mathbf{G}(\cdot,\xi_{k}) is a mini-batch estimator, and then construct G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} as follows:

G~​yk:=G​y¯k+𝐆ℬk​yk−𝐆ℬk​y¯k,{\widetilde{G}y^{k}:=G\bar{y}^{k}+\mathbf{G}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}y^{k}-\mathbf{G}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}\bar{y}^{k},}\vskip-2.15277pt (L-SVRG)

where, for all k≥1k\geq 1, y¯k\bar{y}^{k} is updated by

y¯k:={yk−1with probability​𝐩ky¯k−1with probability​1−𝐩k.{\bar{y}^{k}:=\begin{cases}y^{k-1}&\text{with probability}~\mathbf{p}_{k}\\ \bar{y}^{k-1}&\text{with probability}~1-\mathbf{p}_{k}.\end{cases}}\vskip-2.15277pt (28)

Here, 𝐩k∈(0,1)\mathbf{p}_{k}\in(0,1) is a given Bernoulli probability parameter, and y¯0:=y0\bar{y}^{0}:=y^{0}.

The following lemma shows that G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} satisfies Definition 4.1, whose proof is given in [102].

Lemma 4.2

The estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} constructed by (L-SVRG) such that bk≥bk−1b_{k}\geq b_{k-1} satisfies Definition 4.1 with κk:=𝐩k2\kappa_{k}:=\frac{\mathbf{p}_{k}}{2}, Θk:=4bk​𝐩k\Theta_{k}:=\frac{4}{b_{k}\mathbf{p}_{k}}, δk=0\delta_{k}=0, and Δk:=1bk​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(yk,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y¯k,ξ)‖2]\Delta_{k}:=\frac{1}{b_{k}}\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(y^{k},\xi)-\mathbf{G}(\bar{y}^{k},\xi)\|^{2}\big].

4.1.2 Example 2: SAGA estimator.

SAGA was introduced in [34] for solving finite-sum convex optimization. We apply it to (GE) when GG has a finite-sum structure as in (2).

For given GG in (2), an iterate sequence {yk}k≥0\{y^{k}\}_{k\geq 0}, and a random mini-batch ℬk⊆[n]:={1,⋯,n}\mathcal{B}_{k}\subseteq[n]:=\{1,\cdots,n\} of size bkb_{k} sampled independently across iterations, for k≥1k\geq 1, we update G^ik\widehat{G}_{i}^{k} for all i∈[n]i\in[n] as follows:

G^ik:={Gi​yk−1if​i∈ℬk,G^ik−1if​i∉ℬk(no update).{\widehat{G}_{i}^{k}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{lll}G_{i}y^{k-1}&\text{if}~i\in\mathcal{B}_{k},\\ \widehat{G}_{i}^{k-1}&\text{if}~i\notin\mathcal{B}_{k}\quad\textrm{(no update)}.\end{array}\right.}\vskip-2.15277pt (29)

Then, we construct a SAGA estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} for G​ykGy^{k} as follows:

where Gℬk​yk:=1bk​∑i∈ℬkGi​ykG_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}y^{k}:=\frac{1}{b_{k}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{k}}G_{i}y^{k} and G^ℬkk:=1bk​∑i∈ℬkG^ik\widehat{G}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}^{k}:=\frac{1}{b_{k}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}_{k}}\widehat{G}_{i}^{k}. In this case, we need to store nn component G^ik\widehat{G}^{k}_{i} computed so far for all i∈[n]i\in[n] in a table 𝕋k:=[G^1k,⋯,G^nk]\mathbb{T}_{k}:=[\widehat{G}_{1}^{k},\cdots,\widehat{G}_{n}^{k}] initialized at G^i0:=Gi​y0\widehat{G}_{i}^{0}:=G_{i}y^{0} for all i∈[n]i\in[n]. SAGA requires significant memory to store 𝕋k\mathbb{T}_{k} if nn and pp are both large. We have the following result, whose proof can be found in [102].

Lemma 4.3

The estimator G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} constructed by (SAGA) such that bk−1−bk​bk−14​n≤bk≤bk−1b_{k-1}-\frac{b_{k}b_{k-1}}{4n}\leq b_{k}\leq b_{k-1} satisfies Definition 4.1 with κk:=bk2​n\kappa_{k}:=\frac{b_{k}}{2n}, Θk:=5​nbk2\Theta_{k}:=\frac{5n}{b_{k}^{2}}, δk=0\delta_{k}=0, and Δk:=1n​bk​∑i=1n‖Gi​yk−G^ik‖2\Delta_{k}:=\frac{1}{nb_{k}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}}\|G_{i}y^{k}-\widehat{G}_{i}^{k}\|^{2}.

4.1.3 Example 3: L-SARAH estimator.

SARAH was introduced in [85] for finite-sum convex optimization. Its loopless variant, called L-SARAH, was studied in [38, 67] for convex and nonconvex optimization, and recently in [24, 25, 102] for co-coercive root-finding problems. This estimator is constructed as follows.

Given GG, {yk}\{y^{k}\}, and an i.i.d. sample ℬk⊆[n]\mathcal{B}_{k}\subseteq[n] of size bkb_{k}, we construct G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} as

where 𝐆ℬk​(⋅):=1bk​∑ξk∈ℬk𝐆⁡(⋅,ξk)\mathbf{G}_{\mathcal{B}_{k}}(\cdot):=\frac{1}{b_{k}}\sum_{\xi_{k}\in\mathcal{B}_{k}}\mathbf{G}(\cdot,\xi_{k}), G~​y0:=G​y0\widetilde{G}y^{0}:=Gy^{0}, and 𝐩k∈[𝐩¯,1]\mathbf{p}_{k}\in[\underline{\mathbf{p}},1] is a given Bernoulli switching probability and 𝐩¯∈(0,1)\underline{\mathbf{p}}\in(0,1) is a given lower bound.     limk→∞k2​𝔼​[‖G​xk+vk‖2]=0andlimk→∞k2​𝔼​[‖G​yk−1+vk‖2]=0.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\lim_{k\to\infty}k^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}\big]=0\quad\textrm{and}\quad\lim_{k\to\infty}k^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gy^{k-1}+v^{k}\|^{2}\big]=0.\end{array} (36)
  • (d)\mathrm{(d)}

    ((Iteration-complexity)) For a given ϵ>0\epsilon>0, if 𝒮∞<+∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty}<+\infty, then the number of iterations kk to achieve 𝔼⁡[‖G​xk+vk‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2} is at most 𝒪⁡(1/ϵ)\mathcal{O}\big(1/\epsilon\big). This is also the number of evaluations of Jη​TJ_{\eta T}.

  • (e)\mathrm{(e)}

    ((Almost sure convergence)) The conclusions of Theorem 3.2 still hold in this case.

The constant ss in Theorem 4.5 was left free, provided that s>2s>2. It provides flexibility in choosing its value for adjusting other parameters and theoretical bounds. For example, if we assume that α=0\alpha=0 in (3) and choose s=3s=3, then ω^=2.44336\hat{\omega}=2.44336. Consequently, we have λ^:=127.54687≈0.19053\hat{\lambda}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{27.54687}}\approx 0.19053 and μ^:=(s−2)​λ^8​(s−1)≈0.01191\hat{\mu}:=\frac{(s-2)\hat{\lambda}}{8(s-1)}\approx 0.01191. In this case, the conditions L​ρn≤μ^L\rho_{n}\leq\hat{\mu} and 16​ρn≤η≤λ^L16\rho_{n}\leq\eta\leq\frac{\hat{\lambda}}{L} in Theorem 4.5 hold. The supremum of the admissible stepsize is attained asymptotically as s↓2s\downarrow 2, in which case η≲0.27123L\eta\lesssim\frac{0.27123}{L}. Note that these parameter bounds are not tight, and their range could potentially be improved by further refining our analysis.

Theorem 4.5 only establishes convergence rates for (VAPEG), but does not provide its oracle complexity. It also requires the condition (32) to hold for G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} in Definition 4.1. The iteration-complexity of (VAPEG) for achieving an ϵ\epsilon-solution xkx^{k} in expectation, i.e., 𝔼⁡[‖G​xk+vk‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2} is 𝒪⁡(1/ϵ)\mathcal{O}\big(1/\epsilon\big), improving by a factor of 1ϵ\frac{1}{\epsilon} over its non-accelerated counterparts, including [101].

4.3 Oracle complexity of (VAPEG) using L-SVRG, SAGA, and L-SARAH.

In this subsection, we specify the oracle complexity of (VAPEG) using three concrete estimators: L-SVRG, SAGA, and L-SARAH in Subsection 4.1. The key point is to choose an appropriate distribution 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} and a mini-batch size bkb_{k} to fulfill the condition (32). Note that from Lemmas 4.2, 4.3, and 4.4, since δk=0\delta_{k}=0, we always have 𝒮∞:=∑k=0∞δk=0\mathcal{S}_{\infty}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_{k}=0 for these three estimators. Now, let us start with the Loopless SVRG estimator in (L-SVRG).

𝐩k≥Γ​ηρc​bk+2k+s+1.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathbf{p}_{k}\geq\frac{\Gamma\eta}{\rho_{c}b_{k}}+\frac{2}{k+s+1}.\end{array}

Moreover, to ensure 0<𝐩k≤10<\mathbf{p}_{k}\leq 1, we need to impose bk≥c1​nν≥2​Γ​ηρc≥1b_{k}\geq c_{1}n^{\nu}\geq\frac{2\Gamma\eta}{\rho_{c}}\geq 1, leading to n≥[2​Γ​ηc1​ρc]1/νn\geq\big[\frac{2\Gamma\eta}{c_{1}\rho_{c}}\big]^{1/\nu} as stated. In addition, we also have bk≤nb_{k}\leq n.

Now, from (33) of Theorem 4.5, to guarantee that 𝔼⁡[‖G​xK+vK‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{K}+v^{K}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2}, we need to impose C^02​ℛ^02(K+s)2≤ϵ2\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{C}_{0}^{2}\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{0}^{2}}}{(K+s)^{2}}\leq\epsilon^{2} for C^02:=128​(s−1)(19​s+10)\hat{C}_{0}^{2}:=\frac{128(s-1)}{(19s+10)}. This requirement leads to the choice of K:=⌊C^0​ℛ^0ϵ⌋K:=\big\lfloor\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{C}_{0}\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{0}}}{\epsilon}\big\rfloor. In this case, the expected total number of oracle calls 𝐆\mathbf{G} is 𝔼⁡[𝒯K]=n+𝔼⁡[𝒯^K]\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]=n+\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{K}\big], where nn is the number of evaluations in the first epoch k=0k=0, and 𝒯^K\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{K} is the number of evaluations over the next KK iterations. Then, we can evaluate 𝔼⁡[𝒯^K]\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{K}\big] as

𝔼⁡[𝒯^K]:⁣=∑k=1K[n​𝐩k+2​(1−𝐩k)​b]≤∑k=1K(n​𝐩k+2​b)≤∑k=12​c1​nνΓ−s(Γ​n1−νc1+2​nk+s+1+2​c1​nν)+(K−2​c1​nνΓ)​(2​Γ​n1−νc1+2​c1​nν)≤2​n+2​n​ln⁡(2​c1​nνΓ+2)+4​c12​n2​νΓ+C^0​ℛ^0ϵ​(2​n1−νΓ+2​c1​nν)=𝒪⁡(n​ln⁡(nν)+n2​ν+ℛ^0​(n1−ν+nν)ϵ).\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{K}\big]&:=&\sum_{k=1}^{K}[n\mathbf{p}_{k}+2(1-\mathbf{p}_{k})b]\leq\sum_{k=1}^{K}(n\mathbf{p}_{k}+2b)\\ &\leq&\sum_{k=1}^{\frac{2c_{1}n^{\nu}}{\Gamma}-s}\big(\frac{\Gamma n^{1-\nu}}{c_{1}}+\frac{2n}{k+s+1}+2c_{1}n^{\nu}\big)+\big(K-\frac{2c_{1}n^{\nu}}{\Gamma}\big)\big(\frac{2\Gamma n^{1-\nu}}{c_{1}}+2c_{1}n^{\nu}\big)\\ &\leq&2n+2n\ln\big(\frac{2c_{1}n^{\nu}}{\Gamma}+2\big)+\frac{4c_{1}^{2}n^{2\nu}}{\Gamma}+\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{C}_{0}\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{0}}}{\epsilon}\big(\frac{2n^{1-\nu}}{\Gamma}+2c_{1}n^{\nu}\big)\\ &=&\mathcal{O}\left(n\ln(n^{\nu})+n^{2\nu}+\frac{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\hat{\mathcal{R}}_{0}}(n^{1-\nu}+n^{\nu})}{\epsilon}\right).\end{array}

This expression together with 𝔼⁡[𝒯K]=n+𝔼⁡[𝒯^K]\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]=n+\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{\mathcal{T}}_{K}\big] leads to (44). Finally, if we choose ν=12\nu=\frac{1}{2}, then 𝔼⁡[𝒯K]=𝒪⁡(n​ln⁡(n1/2)+n1/2ϵ)\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]=\mathcal{O}\big(n\ln(n^{1/2})+\frac{n^{1/2}}{\epsilon}\big). □\square

Remark 4.12

Note that both 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} and bkb_{k} selected in Corollaries 4.6, 4.8, and 4.10 aim at achieving the best oracle complexity. Other choices of these parameters still work as long as they satisfy the condition κk≥Γ​ηρc​Θk+2k+s+1\kappa_{k}\geq\frac{\Gamma\eta}{\rho_{c}}\Theta_{k}+\frac{2}{k+s+1} in Theorem 4.5. For instance, the probability 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} in Corollary 4.10 can be fixed at 𝐩k:=Γ​ηc1​ρc​n+2s+1\mathbf{p}_{k}:=\frac{\Gamma\eta}{c_{1}\rho_{c}\sqrt{n}}+\frac{2}{s+1} for all k≥1k\geq 1 and s>2s>2. This choice is more convenient for the implementation of (VAPEG) in practice.

Remark 4.13

Compared with [101], Assumption 1 is more restrictive than the weak-Minty condition in [101]. However, (VAPEG) achieves a better convergence rate by a factor of 1k\frac{1}{k} and better oracle complexity by a factor 1ϵ\frac{1}{\epsilon}. Moreover, (VAPEG) also works with biased estimators. For SARAH, it improves by a factor n1/6n^{1/6} over SVRG and SAGA. Compared to [1, 2, 25], (VAPEG) can work with a class of nonmonotone operators, and its convergence guarantee is in 𝔼⁡[‖G​xK+vK‖2]\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{K}+v^{K}\|^{2}\big], whereas the gap function guarantees in [1, 2] apply only to the monotone case. Therefore, a direct comparison of their oracle complexities is not meaningful because the convergence metrics differ. Nevertheless, since the methods in [1, 2] are non-accelerated, we believe that their convergence rate is at most 𝒪⁡(1/k)\mathcal{O}\big(1/k\big), leading to an oracle complexity worse by a factor of 1ϵ\frac{1}{\epsilon} than ours. Other works such as [33, 100, 102] require stronger assumptions such as [star] co-coercivity and strong quasi-monotonicity, excluding our problems of interest.

Remark 4.14

We only consider the finite-sum case (2) in Corollaries 4.6, 4.8, and 4.10. If we consider the general case G⁡(⋅)=𝔼ξ​[𝐆⁡(⋅,ξ)]G(\cdot)=\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\mathbf{G}(\cdot,\xi)\big], then we can also prove that the expected total number of oracle calls 𝔼⁡[𝒯K]\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big] is at most 𝒪~​(ϵ−3)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-3}) to achieve an ϵ\epsilon-solution. However, we skip this analysis.

5 The Detailed Proofs of Theorems 3.1, 3.2, and 4.5.

For readability, we present the technical proofs of Theorems 3.1, 3.2, and 4.5 in this section.

The proof of Theorem 3.1 is divided into several steps.

5.1.3 The proof of Theorem 3.1.

For clarity, we divide the proof into the following steps.

5.2 The proof of Theorem 3.2: Almost sure convergence.

Similar to the proof of Theorem 3.1, we also divide this proof into several steps as follows.

Step 1 (Almost sure summability bounds). For ℒk\mathcal{L}_{k} given in (54), from (55), we have

ℒk−𝔼k​[ℒk+1]≥ϵ1​η​tk​(tk−s)2​𝔼k​[‖w^k+1−wk‖2]+η​s​tk2​𝔼k​[‖w^k+1‖2]+(s−2)​(4​s−7)​η​(k+1)64​(s−1)​‖wk‖2+(s−2)​η​L2​tk−1232​(s−1)​‖xk−yk−1‖2+(2​s+1)​Λ0​η​(1−κ)​tk−1​(tk−1−s)s2​Δk−1+(s−2)​η​tk−1232​(s−1)​‖ek−1‖2−Λ0​η​δk.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathcal{L}_{k}-\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\mathcal{L}_{k+1}\big]&\geq&\frac{\epsilon_{1}\eta t_{k}(t_{k}-s)}{2}\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|\hat{w}^{k+1}-w^{k}\|^{2}\big]+\frac{\eta st_{k}}{2}\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|\hat{w}^{k+1}\|^{2}\big]\\ &&+{~}\frac{(s-2)(4s-7)\eta(k+1)}{64(s-1)}\|w^{k}\|^{2}+\frac{(s-2)\eta L^{2}t_{k-1}^{2}}{32(s-1)}\|x^{k}-y^{k-1}\|^{2}\\ &&+{~}\frac{(2s+1)\Lambda_{0}\eta{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}(1-\kappa)}t_{k-1}(t_{k-1}-s)}{s^{2}}\Delta_{k-1}+\frac{(s-2)\eta t_{k-1}^{2}}{32(s-1)}\|e^{k-1}\|^{2}-\Lambda_{0}\eta\delta_{k}.\end{array} (66)

Let us define

Uk:⁣=ℒk+ϵ1​η​tk−1​(tk−1−s)2​‖w^k−wk−1‖2+η​s​tk−12​‖w^k‖2.\begin{array}[]{lcl}U_{k}&:=&\mathcal{L}_{k}+\frac{\epsilon_{1}\eta t_{k-1}(t_{k-1}-s)}{2}\|\hat{w}^{k}-w^{k-1}\|^{2}+\frac{\eta st_{k-1}}{2}\|\hat{w}^{k}\|^{2}.\end{array} (67)

Note that ℒk≥0\mathcal{L}_{k}\geq 0 almost surely for all k≥0k\geq 0 and 𝒮∞:=∑k=0∞δk<+∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_{k}<+\infty by our assumption, applying Lemma A.3 to the last inequality, we conclude that limk→∞Uk\lim_{k\to\infty}U_{k} exists almost surely. Moreover, we also have the following almost sure summability bounds:

∑k=0∞(k+s)​‖w^k‖2<+∞,∑k=0∞(k+1)​‖wk‖2<+∞,∑k=0∞(k+s+1)2​‖ek‖2<+∞,∑k=0∞(k+1)​(k+s+1)​Δk<+∞,∑k=0∞(k+1)​(k+s+1)​‖w^k+1−wk‖2<+∞,∑k=0∞(k+s)2​‖xk+1−yk‖2<+∞.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+s)\|\hat{w}^{k}\|^{2}&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)\|w^{k}\|^{2}&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+s+1)^{2}\|e^{k}\|^{2}&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)(k+s+1)\Delta_{k}&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+1)(k+s+1)\|\hat{w}^{k+1}-w^{k}\|^{2}&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(k+s)^{2}\|x^{k+1}-y^{k}\|^{2}&<&+\infty.\end{array} (69)
