From (3) of Assumption 1, for any α∈[0,1)\alpha\in[0,1), we have |∥wk+1−w^k+1|∥2≤L21−α∥xk+1−yk∥2|\!\|w^{k+1}-\hat{w}^{k+1}|\!\|^{2}\leq\frac{L^{2}}{1-\alpha}\|x^{k+1}-y^{k}\|^{2}. Using this bound, the relations |∥⋅|∥≥∥⋅∥|\!\|\cdot|\!\|\geq\|\cdot\|, and 𝔼⁡[‖ek‖2]≤𝔼⁡[Δk]\mathbb{E}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\mathbb{E}\big[\Delta_{k}\big] from the first line of (27) after taking total expectations, we also obtain from (83) that

∑k=0∞tk2𝔼[|∥wk+1−w^k+1|∥2]<+∞,∑k=0∞tk2​𝔼​[‖wk+1−w^k+1‖2]<+∞,∑k=0∞tk2​𝔼​[‖ek‖2]<+∞.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t_{k}^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[|\!\|w^{k+1}-\hat{w}^{k+1}|\!\|^{2}\big]&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t_{k}^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|w^{k+1}-\hat{w}^{k+1}\|^{2}\big]&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t_{k}^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]&<&+\infty.\end{array} (84)

By Young’s inequality, we easily get

‖wk+1−wk‖2≤2​‖wk+1−w^k+1‖2+2​‖w^k+1−wk‖2,‖w^k+1−w^k‖2≤2​‖wk−w^k+1‖2+2​‖wk−w^k‖2.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\|w^{k+1}-w^{k}\|^{2}&\leq&2\|w^{k+1}-\hat{w}^{k+1}\|^{2}+2\|\hat{w}^{k+1}-w^{k}\|^{2},\\ \|\hat{w}^{k+1}-\hat{w}^{k}\|^{2}&\leq&2\|w^{k}-\hat{w}^{k+1}\|^{2}+2\|w^{k}-\hat{w}^{k}\|^{2}.\end{array}

Moreover, we also have 𝔼⁡[‖e^k‖2]≤2​𝔼​[‖ek−1‖2]+2​𝔼​[‖wk−w^k‖2]\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{e}^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq 2\mathbb{E}\big[\|e^{k-1}\|^{2}\big]+2\mathbb{E}\big[\|w^{k}-\hat{w}^{k}\|^{2}\big]. Using these relations, we can obviously derive from (83) and (84) that

∑k=0∞tk2​𝔼​[‖wk+1−wk‖2]<+∞,∑k=0∞tk2​𝔼​[‖w^k+1−w^k‖2]<+∞,∑k=0∞tk2​𝔼​[‖e^k‖2]<+∞.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t_{k}^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|w^{k+1}-w^{k}\|^{2}\big]&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t_{k}^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{w}^{k+1}-\hat{w}^{k}\|^{2}\big]&<&+\infty,\\ \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t_{k}^{2}\mathbb{E}\big[\|\hat{e}^{k}\|^{2}\big]&<&+\infty.\end{array} (85)

Step 5 (Applying Lemmas 5.6 and 5.7). The proof of (36) follows the same arguments as the proof of Step 4 in Theorem 3.1 and we omit the details. The iteration-complexity stated in Statement (d) is also proven as in Theorem 3.1, and we omit it here.

Step 6 (Almost sure convergence). The almost sure convergence results in Statement (e) follow from an argument similar to the proof of Theorem 3.2, and hence we omit the details. □\square

6 Numerical Experiments.

In this section, we present three numerical examples to validate our algorithm, (VAPEG), and compare it with closely related methods. Our Python implementation was run on an Apple M4 MacBook Pro (24 GB RAM, 1 TB SSD).

6.1 Bilinear matrix game: Policeman vs. Burglar problem.

Consider a city with m2m^{2} houses distributed on a grid m×mm\times m, where the jj-th house has wealth wjw_{j} for all j=1,⋯,m2j=1,\cdots,m^{2}. Each night, a Burglar selects a house jj to rob, while a Policeman chooses a location to station himself near house kk. Once the burglary begins, the Policeman is immediately informed of the burglary location, and the probability that he apprehends the Burglar is given by 𝐩c:=exp⁡{−θ​dist​(j,k)}\mathbf{p}_{c}:=\exp\{-\theta\,\mathrm{dist}(j,k)\}, where dist⁡(j,k)\mathrm{dist}(j,k) is the distance between houses jj and kk. However, neither the Burglar nor the Policeman has access to the true wealth wjw_{j}; instead, they need to estimate it using a set of nn observations w^j(i){\hat{w}^{(i)}_{j}} for i∈[n]i\in[n]. The Burglar aims to maximize his expected reward, which is ℛj​k:=1n​∑i=1nw^j(i)​(1−exp⁡{−θ​dist​(j,k)})\mathcal{R}_{jk}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\hat{w}^{(i)}_{j}}\left(1-\exp\{-\theta\,\mathrm{dist}(j,k)\}\right), while the Policeman’s objective is to minimize ℛj​k\mathcal{R}_{jk}.

(a)\mathrm{(a)} Mathematical model. The Policeman vs. Burglar problem described above can be viewed as a zero-sum game. It was studied in [80] and we slightly modify it to obtain a stochastic version. Following [80], we define a payoff matrix 𝐋\mathbf{L} as follows:

𝐋:=1n∑i=1n𝐋(i),𝐋(i)j,k=w^(i)j(1−exp{−θdist(j,k)}),1≤j,k≤m2.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathbf{L}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{L}^{(i)},\quad\mathbf{L}^{(i)}_{j,k}={\hat{w}^{(i)}_{j}}\left(1-\exp\{-\theta\,\mathrm{dist}(j,k)\}\right),\quad 1\leq j,k\leq m^{2}.\end{array}

Then, we can formulate the above problem as the following classical bilinear matrix game:

minu∈Δp1maxv∈Δp2{ℒ(u,v):=⟨𝐋u,v⟩},\min_{u\in\Delta_{p_{1}}}\max_{v\in\Delta_{p_{2}}}\Big\{\mathcal{L}(u,v):=\langle\mathbf{L}u,v\rangle\Big\}, (86)

where uu and vv represent mixed strategies of the Policeman and Burglar, and Δp1\Delta_{p_{1}} and Δp2\Delta_{p_{2}} are the standard simplexes in ℝp1\mathbb{R}^{p_{1}} and ℝp2\mathbb{R}^{p_{2}}, respectively with p1=p2=m2p_{1}=p_{2}=m^{2}.

Let us define x:=[u;v]∈ℝpx:=[u;v]\in\mathbb{R}^{p} with p:=p1+p2p:=p_{1}+p_{2}, Gi​x:=𝐆i​x=[𝐋(i)⊤​v;−𝐋(i)​u]G_{i}x:=\mathbf{G}_{i}x=[\mathbf{L}^{(i)\top}v;-\mathbf{L}^{(i)}u] for i∈[n]i\in[n], and T​x:=[∂δΔp1​(u);∂δΔp2​(v)]Tx:=[\partial\delta_{\Delta_{p_{1}}}(u);\partial\delta_{\Delta_{p_{2}}}(v)], where δ𝒳​(⋅)\delta_{\mathcal{X}}(\cdot) is the indicator of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Then, we can write the optimality condition of (86) as 0∈1n​∑i=1nGi​x+T​x0\in\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}G_{i}x+Tx, a special case of (GE). Since 𝐆:=1n​∑i=1n𝐆i\mathbf{G}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{G}_{i} is a skew-symmetric matrix, GG is monotone and LL-Lipschitz continuous.

(b)\mathrm{(b)} Input data. Following [80], we first choose dist⁡(j,k):=|j−k|\mathrm{dist}(j,k):=|j-k| and θ:=0.8\theta:=0.8. Next, we generate the nominal wealth wjw_{j} from a standard normal distribution, and then take |wj||w_{j}| to ensure its nonnegativity. Then, the noisy wealth wj(i)w^{(i)}_{j} is generated as wj(i):=|wj+ϵj(i)|w^{(i)}_{j}:=|w_{j}+\epsilon^{(i)}_{j}|, where ϵj(i)\epsilon^{(i)}_{j} is a normal random variable with zero mean and variance σ2=0.05\sigma^{2}=0.05. Finally, we produce two sets of experiments, each containing 1010 problem instances, as follows.

  • •

    Experiment 1. m=10m=10 and n=1000n=1000, corresponding to p1=100p_{1}=100 and p=2​p1=200p=2p_{1}=200.

  • •

    Experiment 2. m=15m=15 and n=2000n=2000, corresponding to p1=225p_{1}=225 and p=2​p1=450p=2p_{1}=450.

(c)\mathrm{(c)} Algorithms and parameters. We choose three competitors as follows.

  • •

    The deterministic optimistic gradient method, e.g., in [32], abbreviated by OG. We consider this method as a baseline for our comparison.

  • •

    The variance-reduced forward-reflected-backward splitting algorithm in [2], called VrFRBS.

  • •

    The variance-reduced extragradient (EG) algorithm in [1], abbreviated by VrEG.

Both VrFRBS and VrEG are variants of the EG method and use a Loopless SVRG estimator.

We implement four variants of our method (VAPEG): VAPEG-Sgd, VAPEG-Svrg, VAPEG-Saga, and VAPEG-Sarah, and compare them with OG, VrFRBS, and VrEG. Here, VAPEG-Sgd uses the mini-batch estimator (16), while the last three variants use L-SVRG, SAGA, and L-SARAH estimators, respectively. We run all algorithms for 200 epochs, where each epoch corresponds to nn calls of 𝐆\mathbf{G}.

The parameters of these algorithms are chosen as follows. For all four variants of our methods, we choose η=18​L\eta=\frac{1}{8L}, (i.e., s=3s=3 and ω=7\omega=7). For OG, we choose η=1L\eta=\frac{1}{L}. For VrFRBS, we choose η=0.95​(1−1−𝐩)2​L\eta=\frac{0.95(1-\sqrt{1-\mathbf{p}})}{2L}, and for VrEG, we choose η=0.95​1−αL\eta=\frac{0.95\sqrt{1-\alpha}}{L} with α:=1−𝐩\alpha:=1-\mathbf{p}.

For the probability of reference points and mini-batch size, we choose:

  • •

    𝐩=0.5n−1/3\mathbf{p}=0.5n^{-1/3} for VAPEG-Svrg, VrFRBS, and VrEG. For example, if n=1000n=1000, then 𝐩=0.05\mathbf{p}=0.05, and if n=2000n=2000, then 𝐩=0.04\mathbf{p}=0.04.

  • •

    𝐩=0.5n−1/2\mathbf{p}=0.5n^{-1/2} for VAPEG-Sarah. If n=1000n=1000, then 𝐩=0.016\mathbf{p}=0.016, while if n=2000n=2000, then 𝐩=0.011\mathbf{p}=0.011.

  • •

    bk=⌊0.5​n2/3⌋b_{k}=\lfloor 0.5n^{2/3}\rfloor for VAPEG-Svrg, VAPEG-Saga, VrFRBS, and VrEG. In this case, if n=1000n=1000, then bk=50b_{k}=50, and if n=2000n=2000, then bk=79b_{k}=79.

  • •

    bk=⌊0.5​n1/2⌋b_{k}=\lfloor 0.5n^{1/2}\rfloor for VAPEG-Sarah (e.g., bk=15b_{k}={\color[rgb]{0,0,0}15} for n=1000n=1000 and bk=22b_{k}=22 for n=2000n=2000).

  • •

    For VAPEG-Sgd, we choose increasing mini-batch size bk=max⁡{5,min⁡{0.05​(l+1)3,n}}b_{k}=\max\{5,\min\{0.05(l+1)^{3},n\}\}, where ll is the epoch counter. This choice makes bkb_{k} increasing, but not too fast since bk=𝒪⁡((k+s)3)b_{k}=\mathcal{O}\big((k+s)^{3}\big).

The initial point is chosen as x0:=[1p1⋅ones(p1);1p2⋅ones(p2)]x^{0}:=[\frac{1}{p_{1}}\cdot\texttt{ones($p_{1}$)};\frac{1}{p_{2}}\cdot\texttt{ones($p_{2}$)}] for all methods.

(d)\mathrm{(d)} Numerical results. The results of these experiments are presented in Figure 2.

From Figure 2, we can see that with the theoretical parameters, two VAPEG variants: VAPEG-Saga and VAPEG-Sarah significantly outperform the competitors in both experiments. However, VAPEG-Saga is slightly better than VAPEG-Sarah since VAPEG-Saga uses only one batch ℬk\mathcal{B}_{k} as opposed to two in VAPEG-Sarah per iteration. As a compensation, VAPEG-Saga requires storing a table of nn operator values. Our VAPEG-Svrg also works well, but it is worse than VAPEG-Saga and VAPEG-Sarah. With its theoretical parameters, VrFRBS exhibits the poorest performance among the tested methods. VrEG is still worse than the baseline scheme OG. Our VAPEG-Sgd performs well and better than other methods in early epochs, but then it plateaus at a certain accuracy level, perhaps due to the effect of variance.

Next, we test the effect of the probability 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} and the mini-batch size bkb_{k} of ℬk\mathcal{B}_{k} using the same experiments as in Figure 2. For the methods involving a reference-refresh probability, we halve pkp_{k}, and for the applicable control-variate methods we also halve bkb_{k}; the VAPEG-Sgd batch schedule is left unchanged. Then, the results are presented in Figure 3.

The performance of control-variate methods improves because of the increased number of inner iterations per epoch. This improvement is seen across all variants and consistent with the first test.

6.2 Markov decision processes.

Markov decision processes (MDPs) are commonly used to model sequential decision-making problems [91], with applications in numerous areas such as reinforcement learning [78] and healthcare [3, 47].

(a)\mathrm{(a)} Mathematical model. A finite MDP consists of a state space 𝒮:={1,2,⋯,n}\mathcal{S}:=\{1,2,\cdots,n\} with nn states and a finite action space 𝒜:={1,2,⋯,m}\mathcal{A}:=\{1,2,\cdots,m\} with mm actions. Each state-action pair (s,a)(s,a) is associated with a reward rs​ar_{sa} and a transition probability distribution Ps​a∈ΔnP_{sa}\in\Delta_{n} over the next states. Define r∞:=maxs,a⁡rs​ar_{\infty}:=\max_{s,a}r_{sa}. Without loss of generality, we assume rs​a≥0r_{sa}\geq 0 for all (s,a)∈𝒮×𝒜(s,a)\in\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}. Given a discount factor γ¯∈(0,1)\bar{\gamma}\in(0,1) and an initial state distribution 𝐩0∈Δn\mathbf{p}_{0}\in\Delta_{n}, a common objective in MDPs is to maximize the expected infinite-horizon discounted reward.

Following the same procedure as in [53, 91], this MDP problem can be reformulated into the following convex-concave saddle-point problem:

minv≥0,‖v‖2≤n​r∞1−γ¯maxμ∈Δn​m{ℒ(v,μ):=(1−γ¯)𝐩0⊤v+∑s=1n∑a=1mμs​a(rs​a+γ¯Ps​a⊤v−vs)},{\min_{v\geq 0,\|v\|_{2}\leq\frac{\sqrt{n}r_{\infty}}{1-\bar{\gamma}}}\max\limits_{\mu\in\Delta_{nm}}\Big\{\mathcal{L}(v,\mu):=(1-\bar{\gamma})\mathbf{p}_{0}^{\top}v+\sum\limits_{s=1}^{n}\sum\limits_{a=1}^{m}\mu_{sa}\left(r_{sa}+\bar{\gamma}P_{sa}^{\top}v-v_{s}\right)\Big\},}\vskip-2.15277pt (87)

where v∈ℝnv\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the value-function variable, whose optimal value represents the expected discounted return from each state s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, and μs​a\mu_{sa} (s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} and a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}) are the dual variables.

Next, define x:=[v;μ]∈ℝn⁡(m+1)x:=[v;\mu]\in\mathbb{R}^{n(m+1)} as the concatenation of vv and μ=[μ1;⋯;μn]∈ℝn​m\mu=[\mu_{1};\cdots;\mu_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{nm} (the concatenation of μs\mu_{s}’s with μs=(μs​1,⋯,μs​m)⊤\mu_{s}=(\mu_{s1},\cdots,\mu_{sm})^{\top}, s=1,⋯,ns=1,\cdots,n). For each s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S}, let Bs:=[γ¯​Ps​1−es,⋯,γ¯​Ps​m−es]∈ℝn×mB_{s}:=\left[\bar{\gamma}P_{s1}-e_{s},\cdots,\bar{\gamma}P_{sm}-e_{s}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}, rs:=(rs​1,⋯,rs​m)⊤r_{s}:=(r_{s1},\cdots,r_{sm})^{\top}, ℬn+​(0,R):={v∈ℝ+n:‖v‖2≤R}\mathcal{B}^{+}_{n}(0,R):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}:\|v\|_{2}\leq R\}, and

Gsx:=[n⁡(1−γ¯)​𝐩0,s​es+n​Bs​μs𝟎(s−1)​m−n​rs−n​Bs⊤​v𝟎(n−s)​m],Tx:=[∂δℬn+​(0,n​r∞1−γ¯)​(v)∂δΔn​m​(μ)].{\begin{array}[]{lcl}G_{s}x:=\begin{bmatrix}n(1-\bar{\gamma})\mathbf{p}_{0,s}e_{s}+nB_{s}\mu_{s}\\ \mathbf{0}_{(s-1)m}\\ -nr_{s}-nB_{s}^{\top}v\\ \mathbf{0}_{(n-s)m}\end{bmatrix},\qquad Tx:=\begin{bmatrix}\partial\delta_{\mathcal{B}^{+}_{n}(0,\frac{\sqrt{n}r_{\infty}}{1-\bar{\gamma}})}(v)\\ \partial\delta_{\Delta_{nm}}(\mu)\end{bmatrix}.\end{array}}\vskip-2.15277pt

Then, the optimality condition of (87) can be written as (GE): 0∈G​x+T​x0\in Gx+Tx, where G​x:=1n​∑s=1nGs​xGx:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{s=1}^{n}G_{s}x is a finite-sum representation over the state space 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

(b)\mathrm{(b)} Experimental setup and input data. We evaluate the performance of (VAPEG) on solving problem (87) using randomly generated MDPs from the garnet testbed [5, 17], which is widely used for benchmarking algorithms in sequential decision-making. Garnet MDPs are defined by a branching factor nb/nn_{b}/n, representing the proportion of reachable next states from each (s,a)(s,a) pair. Our setup is characterized by a tuple (|𝒮|,|𝒜|,nb,γ¯)(|\mathcal{S}|,|\mathcal{A}|,n_{b},\bar{\gamma}), and then we consider two experiments: Experiment 1 with (|𝒮|,|𝒜|,nb,γ¯)=(2000,5,1000,0.9)(|\mathcal{S}|,|\mathcal{A}|,n_{b},\bar{\gamma})=(2000,5,1000,0.9), leading to p=12000p=12000 and Experiment 2 with (|𝒮|,|𝒜|,nb,γ¯)=(4000,10,2000,0.9)(|\mathcal{S}|,|\mathcal{A}|,n_{b},\bar{\gamma})=(4000,10,2000,0.9), leading to p=44000p=44000. For each setting, we generate 10 random MDP instances where rewards are sampled uniformly at random from [0,1][0,1].

(c)\mathrm{(c)} Algorithms and parameters. In this experiment, we use three variants of our (VAPEG): VAPEG-Svrg, VAPEG-Saga, and VAPEG-Sarah since they use control variate technique. We again compare them with the baseline method OG, and two other competitors: VrFRBS and VrEG using SVRG estimators. Unlike the previous example, we decide to select the parameters for all algorithms using a grid search procedure on the interval 1LB​[10−5,10]\frac{1}{L_{B}}[10^{-5},10] to search for the best stepsize η\eta in all algorithms, where LB=‖B‖L_{B}=\|B\|. Note that L=LBL=L_{B} is the Lipschitz constant of the aggregate operator GG. Applying this procedure, we obtain the following values of η\eta for each algorithm.

  • •

    For our variants VAPEG-Svrg, VAPEG-Saga, and VAPEG-Sarah, we find η=1103​L\eta=\frac{1}{10^{3}L}.

  • •

    For the baseline method: OG, we get η=1102​L\eta=\frac{1}{10^{2}L}.

  • •

    For VrFRBS, we obtain η=0.95​(1−1−𝐩)102×2​L\eta=\frac{0.95(1-\sqrt{1-\mathbf{p}})}{10^{2}\times 2L}.

  • •

    For VrEG, we find η=0.95​1−α103​L\eta=\frac{0.95\sqrt{1-\alpha}}{10^{3}L} with α:=1−𝐩\alpha:=1-\mathbf{p}.

As in the first example, we still choose 𝐩=0.5n−1/3\mathbf{p}=0.5n^{-1/3} and b=⌊0.5​n2/3⌋b=\lfloor 0.5n^{2/3}\rfloor for VAPEG-Svrg, VrFRBS, and VrEG, 𝐩=0.5n−1/2\mathbf{p}=0.5n^{-1/2} and b=⌊0.5​n1/2⌋b=\lfloor 0.5n^{1/2}\rfloor for VAPEG-Sarah. The initial point is chosen as x0:=[1−γ¯r∞​ones(n);1n​m​ones(nm)]x^{0}:=[\frac{1-\bar{\gamma}}{r_{\infty}}\texttt{ones(n)};\frac{1}{n{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m}}\texttt{ones(n{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}m})}] for all methods.

(d)\mathrm{(d)} Numerical results. We run all the algorithms using the above setting on two experiments, and the results are shown in Figure 4.

As shown in Figure 4, the three VAPEG variants: VAPEG-Svrg, VAPEG-Saga, and VAPEG-Sarah, consistently outperform both the baseline method (OG) and competing algorithms across the entire training horizon. Among them, VAPEG-Svrg achieves the worst residual norm, while VAPEG-Sarah demonstrates the best overall performance. These results suggest that acceleration indeed provides a significant performance boost.

Finally, we examine the effect of the probability 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} and the mini-batch size bkb_{k} on the performance of our methods by halving their values to obtain more inner iterations in each epoch. The corresponding results are presented in Figure 5.

We observe that the three variants of (VAPEG) outperform their non-accelerated counterparts. A smaller mini-batch size bkb_{k} enables our algorithms to run more iterations, while a smaller probability 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} reduces the number of full evaluations of GG. Consequently, both factors contribute to the speedup of the algorithms observed in Figure 5.

6.3 Sparse soft-robust bond portfolio construction.

In this example, we compare our algorithms with three competing methods on a sparse soft-robust bond portfolio construction problem. The model is adapted from the robust bond portfolio formulation in [18, Section 6.2].

(a)\mathrm{(a)} Mathematical model. Consider a portfolio of mm bonds with quantities z=(z1,⋯,zm)∈𝒵⊆ℝ+mz=(z_{1},\cdots,z_{m})\in\mathcal{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}_{+} over time periods t=1,⋯,Tt=1,\cdots,T. A market state is modeled by q=(qu,qs)∈ℝT+mq=(q^{u},q^{s})\in\mathbb{R}^{T+m}, where qu=(q1u,⋯,qTu)∈ℝTq^{u}=(q^{u}_{1},\cdots,q^{u}_{T})\in\mathbb{R}^{T} is the yield curve and qs=(q1s,⋯,qms)∈ℝ+mq^{s}=(q^{s}_{1},\cdots,q^{s}_{m})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{+} is the bond spread. For a market state q=(qu,qs)q=(q^{u},q^{s}), let π∈ℝ+m\pi\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{+} denote the bond prices, where the price πj\pi_{j} of bond jj is modeled by πj​(q):=∑t=1Tαj,t​exp⁡(−t⁡(qtu+qjs))\pi_{j}(q):=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{j,t}\exp\big(-t(q^{u}_{t}+q^{s}_{j})\big), with αj,t≥0\alpha_{j,t}\geq 0 denoting the cash flow paid by bond jj at time tt.

Next, fix a reference market state q¯\bar{q} to evaluate local bond-price sensitivities, and let y:=(u⊤,s⊤)⊤∈ℝT+my:=(u^{\top},s^{\top})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T+m} denote changes in yields and spreads relative to this state. Thus, the stressed state is q¯+y\bar{q}+y. Since π\pi is highly nonlinear, we approximate it around q¯\bar{q} by π⁡(q¯+y)≈π⁡(q¯)+Jπ​(q¯)​y\pi(\bar{q}+y)\approx\pi(\bar{q})+J_{\pi}(\bar{q})y, where JπJ_{\pi} is the Jacobian of the bond-price map at q¯\bar{q}. Denoting B:=−Jπ​(q¯)B:=-J_{\pi}(\bar{q}), we obtain π​(q¯+y)⊤​z≈π​(q¯)⊤​z−z⊤​B​y\pi(\bar{q}+y)^{\top}z\approx\pi(\bar{q})^{\top}z-z^{\top}By. Let ϕ:ℝm→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R} be a smooth convex nominal portfolio objective, which may include tracking error against a benchmark, risk, or transaction cost terms. Absorbing the reference-state portfolio value, we define f⁡(z):=ϕ⁡(z)−π​(q¯)⊤​zf(z):=\phi(z)-\pi(\bar{q})^{\top}z, which remains smooth and convex.

Now, instead of using a bounded uncertainty set together with a nonsmooth uncertainty penalty, we penalize the overall magnitude of the market shock and its movements along prescribed market-shock patterns through

h⁡(y):⁣=γ2​‖y‖2+ν​∑ℓ=1rlog⁡cosh⁡(cℓ⊤​y),\begin{array}[]{lcl}h(y)&:=&\frac{\gamma}{2}\|y\|^{2}+\nu\sum_{\ell=1}^{r}\log\cosh(c_{\ell}^{\top}y),\end{array} (88)

where γ>0\gamma>0, ν>0\nu>0, and C∈ℝr×(T+m)C\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times(T+m)} has rows cℓ⊤c_{\ell}^{\top}, ℓ∈[r]\ell\in[r]. Each vector cℓc_{\ell} represents a prescribed pattern of joint movements in yields and spreads, while cℓ⊤​yc_{\ell}^{\top}y measures the signed projection of the market shock onto that pattern. Since log⁡cosh⁡(⋅)\log\cosh(\cdot) is even and increasing in the absolute value of its argument, the second term penalizes large movements along these patterns. The parameter γ\gamma controls the overall magnitude penalty, while ν\nu controls the strength of the pattern-specific penalty.

Finally, to promote a sparse bond portfolio, we use the SCAD penalty ℛλ,θ​(z):=∑j=1mRλ,θ​(zj)\mathcal{R}_{\lambda,\theta}(z):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}R_{\lambda,\theta}(z_{j}) proposed in [42] as a continuous surrogate for cardinality. The resulting sparse soft-robust bond portfolio model is the following nonconvex-concave minimax problem:

minz∈𝒵maxy∈ℝT+m{ℒ(z,y):=f(z)+z⊤By−h(y)+τℛλ,θ(z)}\min_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{T+m}}\left\{\mathcal{L}(z,y):=f(z)+z^{\top}By-h(y)+\tau\mathcal{R}_{\lambda,\theta}(z)\right\} (89)

Here, λ>0\lambda>0 determines the SCAD threshold, θ>2\theta>2 is the SCAD shape parameter, and τ>0\tau>0 controls the strength of the sparsity regularization. The SCAD penalty can be decomposed as Rλ,θ​(t)=λ​|t|−R~λ,θ​(t)R_{\lambda,\theta}(t)=\lambda|t|-\tilde{R}_{\lambda,\theta}(t), where

R~λ,θ​(t)={0,|t|≤λ,(|t|−λ)22​(θ−1),λ<|t|≤θ​λ,λ​|t|−(θ+1)​λ22,|t|>θ​λ.\tilde{R}_{\lambda,\theta}(t)=\begin{cases}0,&|t|\leq\lambda,\\[2.84526pt] \dfrac{(|t|-\lambda)^{2}}{2(\theta-1)},&\lambda<|t|\leq\theta\lambda,\\[5.69054pt] \lambda|t|-\dfrac{(\theta+1)\lambda^{2}}{2},&|t|>\theta\lambda.\end{cases} (90)

Let ℛ~λ,θ​(z):=∑j=1mR~λ,θ​(zj)\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\tilde{R}_{\lambda,\theta}(z_{j}). Then, the saddle-point problem (89) can be written equivalently as

minz∈ℝmmaxy∈ℝT+m{ℒ(z,y):=f(z)+z⊤By−h(y)−τℛ~λ,θ(z)+τλ∥z∥1+δ𝒵(z)},\min_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\max_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{T+m}}\left\{\mathcal{L}(z,y):=f(z)+z^{\top}By-h(y)-\tau\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z)+\tau\lambda\|z\|_{1}+\delta_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)\right\}, (91)

where δ𝒵\delta_{\mathcal{Z}} is the indicator function of the closed convex set 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Suppose f⁡(z)=1n​∑i=1nfi​(z)f(z)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(z), where every fif_{i} is continuously differentiable. Now, let us define

x=[zy],Gix:=[∇fi(z)+By−τ∇ℛ~λ,θ(z)∇h​(y)−B⊤​z],andTx:=[τ​λ​∂‖z‖1+∂δ𝒵​(z)0].x=\begin{bmatrix}z\\ y\end{bmatrix},\qquad G_{i}x:=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f_{i}(z)+By-\tau\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z)\\ \nabla h(y)-B^{\top}z\end{bmatrix},\quad\text{and}\quad Tx:=\begin{bmatrix}\tau\lambda\partial\|z\|_{1}+\partial\delta_{\mathcal{Z}}(z)\\ 0\end{bmatrix}. (92)

Then, the optimality condition of (91) can be written as 0∈G​x+T​x0\in Gx+Tx, where G​x:=1n​∑i=1nGi​xGx:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}G_{i}x.

Proposition 6.1 summarizes the properties of GG and TT, with its proof deferred to Appendix C.6.

Proposition 6.1

Suppose that ff in (91) is convex and LfL_{f}-average smooth, i.e.:

1n​∑i=1n‖∇fi​(z)−∇fi​(z′)‖2≤Lf2​‖z−z′‖2,∀z,z′∈ℝm.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\nabla f_{i}(z)-\nabla f_{i}(z^{\prime})\|^{2}\leq L_{f}^{2}\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2},\qquad\forall z,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}.\end{array}

(b)\mathrm{(b)} Data generation. This example aims to illustrate the performance of our methods and their competitors on a nonmonotone problem. The data is generated synthetically as follows.

(i)\mathrm{(i)} Bond cash flows and reference market state. For each bond j∈[m]j\in[m], we independently generate its maturity and coupon rate according to Mj∼Unif⁡{2,⋯,T}M_{j}\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{2,\cdots,T\} and κj∼Unif⁡[0.018,0.042]\kappa_{j}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0.018,0.042], respectively. The face value is normalized to one, and the cash flows are αj,t:=κj𝟏{t≤Mj}+𝟏{t=Mj}\alpha_{j,t}:=\kappa_{j}\boldsymbol{1}_{\{t\leq M_{j}\}}+\boldsymbol{1}_{\{t=M_{j}\}}. The reference yield curve is deterministic, q¯tu:=0.018+0.012T−1​(t−1)\bar{q}_{t}^{u}:=0.018+\frac{0.012}{T-1}(t-1), t∈[T]t\in[T], while the bond-specific reference spreads are independently generated from q¯js∼Unif⁡[0.004,0.007]\bar{q}_{j}^{s}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0.004,0.007], j∈[m]j\in[m]. Once the reference market state q¯\bar{q} is generated, the matrix B=−Jπ​(q¯)∈ℝm×(T+m)B=-J_{\pi}(\bar{q})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times(T+m)} is constructed analytically. Specifically, the yield-curve and spread blocks of BB are given by

Bj,t=t​αj,t​exp⁡(−t⁡(q¯tu+q¯js)),t∈[T],Bj,T+ℓ=𝟏{j=ℓ}∑t=1Ttαj,texp(−t(q¯tu+q¯js)),ℓ∈[m].\begin{array}[]{lcll}B_{j,t}&=&t\alpha_{j,t}\exp\bigl(-t(\bar{q}_{t}^{u}+\bar{q}_{j}^{s})\bigr),&\qquad t\in[T],\\ B_{j,T+\ell}&=&\mathbf{1}_{\{j=\ell\}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}t\alpha_{j,t}\exp\bigl(-t(\bar{q}_{t}^{u}+\bar{q}_{j}^{s})\bigr),&\qquad\ell\in[m].\end{array}

Since the spread block is diagonal with strictly positive diagonal entries, every generated matrix BB has full row rank, and thus σ:=σmin​(B⊤)>0\sigma:=\sigma_{\min}(B^{\top})>0.

(ii)\mathrm{(ii)} Market-stress directions. For each setting, define 𝒕:=(1,2,⋯,T)⊤\boldsymbol{t}:=(1,2,\cdots,T)^{\top}, 𝟏T:=(1,⋯,1)⊤∈ℝT\boldsymbol{1}_{T}:=(1,\cdots,1)^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}, t¯:=T+12\bar{t}:=\frac{T+1}{2}, and 𝒕~:=𝒕−t¯​ 1T\widetilde{\boldsymbol{t}}:=\boldsymbol{t}-\bar{t}\,\boldsymbol{1}_{T}. The level, slope, and curvature directions and the common credit-spread direction are defined as

clev:=𝟏TT,cslp:=𝒕~‖𝒕~‖,ccurv:=𝒕~⊙2−‖𝒕~‖2T​𝟏T‖𝒕~⊙2−‖𝒕~‖2T​𝟏T‖,andcspr:=𝟏mm,\begin{array}[]{lcl}c^{\mathrm{lev}}:=\frac{\boldsymbol{1}_{T}}{\sqrt{T}},\qquad c^{\mathrm{slp}}:=\frac{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{t}}}{\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{t}}\|},\qquad c^{\mathrm{curv}}:=\frac{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{t}}^{\odot 2}-\frac{\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{t}}\|^{2}}{T}\boldsymbol{1}_{T}}{\big\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{t}}^{\odot 2}-\frac{\|\widetilde{\boldsymbol{t}}\|^{2}}{T}\boldsymbol{1}_{T}\big\|},\qquad\text{and}\qquad c^{\mathrm{spr}}:=\frac{\boldsymbol{1}_{m}}{\sqrt{m}},\end{array}

respectively, where ⊙2 denotes the elementwise square. We then set

C:=[(clev)⊤0(cslp)⊤0(ccurv)⊤00(cspr)⊤]∈ℝ4×(T+m).C:=\begin{bmatrix}(c^{\mathrm{lev}})^{\top}&0\\ (c^{\mathrm{slp}})^{\top}&0\\ (c^{\mathrm{curv}})^{\top}&0\\ 0&(c^{\mathrm{spr}})^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{4\times(T+m)}.

The four rows of CC are orthonormal, and hence ‖C‖=1\|C\|=1. We use ν=1\nu=1 and γ:=ν​‖C‖2=1\gamma:=\nu\|C\|^{2}=1. Thus, Lh=γ+ν​‖C‖2=2L_{h}=\gamma+\nu\|C\|^{2}=2.

(iii)\mathrm{(iii)} Finite-sum scenarios. The shifted portfolio objective is chosen as f⁡(z):=1n​∑i=1nfi​(z)f(z):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}(z), where fi​(z):=12​(gi⊤​z−ri)2+μ2​‖z‖2+b⊤​zf_{i}(z):=\frac{1}{2}(g_{i}^{\top}z-r_{i})^{2}+\frac{\mu}{2}\|z\|^{2}+b^{\top}z. Here, gi∈ℝmg_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} represents the modeled bond responses in scenario ii, so that gi⊤​zg_{i}^{\top}z is the aggregate portfolio response, while ri∈ℝr_{i}\in\mathbb{R} is the corresponding benchmark response. Thus, the first term is the average squared tracking error, while the remaining terms provide quadratic regularization and a linear portfolio adjustment.

Suppose that each market scenario is characterized by a 66-dimensional factor model. We first define the standardized bond features

M^j:=Mj−M¯sdM,κ^j:=κj−κ¯sdκ,s^j:=q¯js−s¯sds,\begin{array}[]{lcl}\widehat{M}_{j}:=\frac{M_{j}-\bar{M}}{\mathrm{sd}_{M}},\qquad\widehat{\kappa}_{j}:=\frac{\kappa_{j}-\bar{\kappa}}{\mathrm{sd}_{\kappa}},\qquad\widehat{s}_{j}:=\frac{\bar{q}_{j}^{s}-\bar{s}}{\mathrm{sd}_{s}},\end{array}

F^j,::=[1,M^j,M^j2−1m∑ℓ=1mM^ℓ2,κ^j,s^j,M^js^j].\begin{array}[]{lcl}\widehat{F}_{j,:}:=\big[1,\ \widehat{M}_{j},\ \widehat{M}_{j}^{2}-\frac{1}{m}\sum_{\ell=1}^{m}\widehat{M}_{\ell}^{2},\ \widehat{\kappa}_{j},\ \widehat{s}_{j},\ \widehat{M}_{j}\widehat{s}_{j}\big].\end{array}

We use the same SCAD and box-constraint parameters for all instances: 𝒵=[0,1]m\mathcal{Z}=[0,1]^{m}, λ=0.25\lambda=0.25, and θ=2.5\theta=2.5. The parameters τ\tau and μ\mu are selected as follows. Therefore, we get

⟨wε−w⋆,xε−x⋆⟩=(μ−τθ−1)​‖zε−z⋆‖2<0\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle w^{\varepsilon}-w^{\star},x^{\varepsilon}-x^{\star}\rangle&=&\big(\mu-\frac{\tau}{\theta-1}\big)\|z^{\varepsilon}-z^{\star}\|^{2}<0\end{array}

due to the choice μ=τ4​(θ−1)<τθ−1\mu=\frac{\tau}{4(\theta-1)}<\frac{\tau}{\theta-1}. Since ε\varepsilon can be chosen arbitrarily small, the last inequality shows that Φ\Phi fails to be monotone in every neighborhood of x⋆x^{\star}.

(c)\mathrm{(c)} Experiment setup and algorithms. Our setup is characterized by a tuple (n,m,T)(n,m,T), with two experiments: (n,m,T)=(1000,200,20)(n,m,T)=(1000,200,20), leading to p=420p=420, and (n,m,T)=(2000,460,30)(n,m,T)=(2000,460,30), leading to p=950p=950. For each setting, we generate 10 random problem instances as described above. We test four variants of our (VAPEG) and compare them with the same three benchmarks as before. The parameters are chosen as in Subsection 6.1. For all algorithms, the initial point is chosen as x0=[z0,𝟎]x^{0}=[z^{0},\mathbf{0}], where z0z^{0} is sampled i.i.d. from 𝒰⁡(1.1​λ,0.9​θ​λ)\mathcal{U}(1.1\lambda,0.9\theta\lambda), so that every portfolio component lies strictly inside the concave region of the SCAD penalty.

(d)\mathrm{(d)} Numerical results. The results of these experiments are reported in Figure 6.

Unlike the bilinear matrix game problem considered in Subsection 6.1, whose associated operator is monotone, the soft-robust bond-portfolio problem is genuinely nonmonotone due to the concave part of the SCAD penalty. Moreover, by construction, the problem remains nonmonotone around the stationary point. Nevertheless, the performance of the algorithms remains largely consistent across the two experiments. In both experiments, VAPEG-Saga and VAPEG-Sarah converge substantially faster and attain significantly higher accuracy than the other methods, reaching relative residuals of approximately 10−810^{-8}, with VAPEG-Sarah performing slightly better than VAPEG-Saga. VAPEG-Svrg also performs relatively well, reaching a final residual of roughly 10−610^{-6}, whereas VAPEG-Sgd also reaches the magnitude of 10−610^{-6}. Meanwhile, OG converges more slowly, and the two benchmark methods, VrFRBS and VrEG, exhibit the slowest residual decay. These results suggest that the advantages of the proposed variance-reduced schemes persist beyond the monotone setting and extend to structured nonmonotone finite-sum inclusions.

Appendix A Preliminary Results and Example Verification.

This appendix provides useful lemmas. It also verifies the examples in Subsection 2.4.

A.1 Useful lemmas.

We recall some useful results which will be used in our analysis.

Lemma A.1 ([11], Lemma 5.31)

Let {uk}\{u_{k}\}, {vk}\{v_{k}\}, {γk}\{\gamma_{k}\}, and {εk}\{\varepsilon_{k}\} be nonnegative sequences such that A∞:=∑k=0∞γk<+∞A_{\infty}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma_{k}<+\infty and B∞:=∑k=0∞εk<+∞B_{\infty}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon_{k}<+\infty. In addition, we assume that

uk+1≤(1+γk)​uk−vk+εk,for all k≥0.u_{k+1}\leq(1+\gamma_{k})u_{k}-v_{k}+\varepsilon_{k},\quad\textrm{for all $k\geq 0$}. (93)

Then, we conclude that limk→∞uk\lim_{k\to\infty}u_{k} exists and ∑k=0∞vk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}v_{k}<+\infty.

Lemma A.2 ([102])

Given a nonnegative sequence {uk}\{u_{k}\} and ω≥0\omega\geq 0 such that limk→∞kω+1​uk\lim_{k\to\infty}k^{\omega+1}u^{k} exists and ∑k=0∞kω​uk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k^{\omega}u_{k}<+\infty. Then, we conclude that limk→∞kω+1​uk=0\lim_{k\to\infty}k^{\omega+1}u^{k}=0.

We also need the well-known Robbins-Siegmund supermartingale theorem [93].

Lemma A.3 ([93])

Let {Uk}\{U_{k}\}, {αk}\{\alpha_{k}\}, {Vk}\{V_{k}\} and {Rk}\{R_{k}\} be sequences of nonnegative integrable random variables on some arbitrary probability space and adapted to the filtration {ℱk}\left\{\mathcal{F}_{k}\right\} with ∑k=0∞αk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\alpha_{k}<+\infty and ∑k=0∞Rk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}R_{k}<+\infty almost surely, and

𝔼⁡[Uk+1∣ℱk]≤(1+αk)​Uk−Vk+Rk,\mathbb{E}\big[U_{k+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}\big]\leq(1+\alpha_{k})U_{k}-V_{k}+R_{k}, (94)

almost surely for all k≥0k\geq 0. Then, almost surely, {Uk}\{U_{k}\} converges to a nonnegative random variable UU and ∑k=0∞Vk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}V_{k}<+\infty almost surely.

The following lemma is proven similarly to [30, Theorem 3.2.] and [33, Proposition 4.1.]. We recall it here without repeating the proof to cover the composite mapping Φ\Phi in (GE).

Lemma A.4

Suppose that gra⁡(Φ)\mathrm{gra}(\Phi) in (GE) is closed and zer⁡(Φ)≠∅\mathrm{zer}(\Phi)\neq\emptyset. Let {xk}\{x^{k}\} be a sequence of random vectors such that for all x⋆∈zer⁡(Φ)x^{\star}\in\mathrm{zer}(\Phi), {‖xk−x⋆‖2}\{\|x^{k}-x^{\star}\|^{2}\} almost surely converges to a [0,∞)[0,\infty)-valued random variable. In addition, assume that {‖wk‖}\{\|w^{k}\|\} for (xk,wk)∈gra⁡(Φ)(x^{k},w^{k})\in\mathrm{gra}(\Phi) also almost surely converges to zero. Then, {xk}\{x^{k}\} almost surely converges to a zer⁡(Φ)\mathrm{zer}(\Phi)-valued random variable x⋆∈zer⁡(Φ)x^{\star}\in\mathrm{zer}(\Phi).

A.2 Verifying Example 3 in Subsection 2.3

We verify the co-hypomonotonicity of the operator in Example 3 from Subsection 2.3. For any x,y∈dom⁡(A)x,y\in\mathrm{dom}(A), let wx∈A​xw_{x}\in Ax and wy∈A​yw_{y}\in Ay. Then, u:=−ρ−1​x−wx∈T​xu:=-\rho^{-1}x-w_{x}\in Tx and v:=−ρ−1​y−wy∈T​yv:=-\rho^{-1}y-w_{y}\in Ty. Therefore, we have

⟨u−v,x−y⟩=−ρ−1​‖x−y‖2−⟨wx−wy,x−y⟩,ρ​‖u−v‖2=ρ​‖ρ−1​(x−y)+(wx−wy)‖2=ρ−1​‖x−y‖2+2​⟨wx−wy,x−y⟩+ρ​‖wx−wy‖2.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle u-v,x-y\rangle&=&-\rho^{-1}\|x-y\|^{2}-\langle w_{x}-w_{y},x-y\rangle,\\ \rho\|u-v\|^{2}&=&\rho\|\rho^{-1}(x-y)+(w_{x}-w_{y})\|^{2}=\rho^{-1}\|x-y\|^{2}+2\langle w_{x}-w_{y},x-y\rangle+\rho\|w_{x}-w_{y}\|^{2}.\end{array}

Adding these two identities gives ⟨u−v,x−y⟩+ρ​‖u−v‖2=⟨wx−wy,x−y⟩+ρ​‖wx−wy‖2≥0\langle u-v,x-y\rangle+\rho\|u-v\|^{2}=\langle w_{x}-w_{y},x-y\rangle+\rho\|w_{x}-w_{y}\|^{2}\geq 0, where the inequality follows from the monotonicity of AA and ρ>0\rho>0. Consequently, ⟨u−v,x−y⟩≥−ρ​‖u−v‖2\langle u-v,x-y\rangle\geq-\rho\|u-v\|^{2} for all (x,u),(y,v)∈gra⁡(T)(x,u),(y,v)\in\mathrm{gra}(T), showing that TT is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone. □\square

A.3 Verifying examples in Subsection 2.4.

We present more details of Subsection 2.4.

Example 2. We provide a more detailed explanation of Example 2 in Subsection 2.4. First, using Jensen’s inequality, it is easy to check that GG satisfies (3) in Assumption 1 with α=1\alpha=1. Second, for all x,y∈dom⁡(Φ)x,y\in\mathrm{dom}(\Phi), let wx:=G​x+vxw_{x}:=Gx+v_{x} and wy:=G​y+vyw_{y}:=Gy+v_{y}, where vx∈T​xv_{x}\in Tx and vy∈T​yv_{y}\in Ty, respectively. Then, from Young’s inequality, we have (1+τ)​‖G​x−G​y‖2−‖vx−vy‖2≥−(1+τ)τ​‖wx−wy‖2(1+\tau)\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}-\|v_{x}-v_{y}\|^{2}\geq-\frac{(1+\tau)}{\tau}\|w_{x}-w_{y}\|^{2} for any τ>0\tau>0. Utilizing the assumptions in [100, 102], Jensen’s inequality, and the last relation, we can easily prove that

⟨wx−wy,x−y⟩=⟨G​x−G​y,x−y⟩+⟨vx−vy,x−y⟩≥1L​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]−ρ​‖vx−vy‖2≥[1L−(1+τ)​ρ]​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]+ρ⁡[(1+τ)​‖G​x−G​y‖2−‖vx−vy‖2]≥[1L−(1+τ)​ρ]​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]−(1+τ)​ρτ​‖wx−wy‖2.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle w_{x}-w_{y},x-y\rangle&=&\langle Gx-Gy,x-y\rangle+\langle v_{x}-v_{y},x-y\rangle\\ &\geq&\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]-\rho\|v_{x}-v_{y}\|^{2}\\ &\geq&\big[\frac{1}{L}-(1+\tau)\rho\big]\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]+\rho\big[(1+\tau)\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}-\|v_{x}-v_{y}\|^{2}\big]\\ &\geq&\big[\frac{1}{L}-(1+\tau)\rho\big]\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]-\frac{(1+\tau)\rho}{\tau}\|w_{x}-w_{y}\|^{2}.\end{array}

This inequality shows that Φ:=G+T\Phi:=G+T studied in [100, 102] satisfies (6) in Assumption 1 with ρn:=(1+τ)​ρτ≥0\rho_{n}:=\frac{(1+\tau)\rho}{\tau}\geq 0, 0≤ρc≤1L−(1+τ)​ρ0\leq\rho_{c}\leq\frac{1}{L}-(1+\tau)\rho. Clearly, to guarantee ρc≥0\rho_{c}\geq 0, we require 0≤L​ρ≤11+τ<10\leq L\rho\leq\frac{1}{1+\tau}<1.

Example 4. Since R⁡(x,y)≤MR(x,y)\leq M, we have n​∑i=1n‖Gi​x−Gi​y‖2≤M​‖∑i=1n(Gi​x−Gi​y)‖2n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|G_{i}x-G_{i}y\|^{2}\leq M\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(G_{i}x-G_{i}y)\|^{2}. It implies that 𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2]=1n​∑i=1n‖Gi​x−Gi​y‖2≤Mn2​‖∑i=1n(Gi​x−Gi​y)‖2=M​‖G​x−G​y‖2\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big]=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|G_{i}x-G_{i}y\|^{2}\leq\frac{M}{n^{2}}\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}(G_{i}x-G_{i}y)\|^{2}=M\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}.
Now, since GG is ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone, we have

⟨G​x−G​y,x−y⟩≥−ρ​‖G​x−G​y‖2=−ρn​‖G​x−G​y‖2+(ρn−ρ)​‖G​x−G​y‖2≥−ρn​‖G​x−G​y‖2+ρn−ρM​𝔼ξ​[‖𝐆⁡(x,ξ)−𝐆⁡(y,ξ)‖2].\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle Gx-Gy,x-y\rangle&\geq&-\rho\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}=-\rho_{n}\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}+(\rho_{n}-\rho)\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}\\ &\geq&-\rho_{n}\|Gx-Gy\|^{2}+\frac{\rho_{n}-\rho}{M}\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\big[\|\mathbf{G}(x,\xi)-\mathbf{G}(y,\xi)\|^{2}\big].\end{array}

C.5 The proof of Corollary 3.4: Oracle complexity of VAPEG using (16).

Assume that G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} satisfies the condition (15) with κ=1\kappa=1, Θ=0\Theta=0, and δk:=δtk1+ν\delta_{k}:=\frac{\delta}{t_{k}^{1+\nu}} for a given δ>0\delta>0 and ν>0\nu>0. Then, we have 𝒮∞:=∑k=0∞δk=δ​∑k=0∞1(k+s+1)1+ν<+∞\mathcal{S}_{\infty}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_{k}=\delta\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(k+s+1)^{1+\nu}}<+\infty. Moreover, by (15) we also have 𝔼k​[‖ek‖2]≤δktk2=δtk3+ν\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\delta_{k}}{t_{k}^{2}}=\frac{\delta}{t_{k}^{3+\nu}}. However, since G~​yk\widetilde{G}y^{k} is constructed by (16), we have 𝔼k​[‖ek‖2]≤σ2bk\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b_{k}}, where σ2\sigma^{2} is the variance bound in Assumption 1. Therefore, the condition 𝔼k​[‖ek‖2]≤δtk3+ν\mathbb{E}_{k}\big[\|e^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\frac{\delta}{t_{k}^{3+\nu}} holds if we impose σ2bk≤δtk3+ν\frac{\sigma^{2}}{b_{k}}\leq\frac{\delta}{t_{k}^{3+\nu}}. Hence, we can choose bk:=⌈σ2​tk3+νδ⌉=⌈σ2​(k+s+1)3+νδ⌉b_{k}:=\big\lceil\frac{\sigma^{2}t_{k}^{3+\nu}}{\delta}\big\rceil=\big\lceil\frac{\sigma^{2}(k+s+1)^{3+\nu}}{\delta}\big\rceil as stated. In this case, the expected total number of oracle calls 𝐆\mathbf{G} is at most

𝔼⁡[𝒯K]:⁣=∑k=0Kbk≤σ2δ​∑k=0K(k+s+1)3+ν=𝒪⁡(σ2​K4+νδ).\begin{array}[]{lcl}\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]&:=&\sum_{k=0}^{K}b_{k}\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\delta}\sum_{k=0}^{K}(k+s+1)^{3+\nu}=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}K^{4+\nu}}{\delta}\big).\end{array}

By (22) of Theorem 3.1, the number of iterations KK to reach an ϵ\epsilon-solution in expectation is K=𝒪⁡(ϵ−1)K=\mathcal{O}\left(\epsilon^{-1}\right). Therefore, we obtain 𝔼⁡[𝒯K]=𝒪⁡(σ2δ​ϵ4+ν)\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\delta\epsilon^{4+\nu}}\big) as stated. Alternatively, if we choose bk:=⌈σ2​(k+s+1)3​log⁡(k+s+1)δ⌉b_{k}:=\big\lceil\frac{\sigma^{2}(k+s+1)^{3}\log(k+s+1)}{\delta}\big\rceil, then 𝒮K:=δ​∑k=0K1(k+s+1)​log⁡(k+s+1)≤1+log⁡(log⁡(K+s+1))\mathcal{S}_{K}:=\delta\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{1}{(k+s+1)\log(k+s+1)}\leq 1+\log(\log(K+s+1)). Hence, from (22) of Theorem 3.1, to achieve 𝔼⁡[‖G​xk+vk‖2]≤ϵ2\mathbb{E}\big[\|Gx^{k}+v^{k}\|^{2}\big]\leq\epsilon^{2}, we require C0​(ℛ02+Λ0​SK)(K+s+1)2≤ϵ2\frac{C_{0}(\mathcal{R}_{0}^{2}+\Lambda_{0}S_{K})}{(K+s+1)^{2}}\leq\epsilon^{2}. Using the upper bound of 𝒮K\mathcal{S}_{K}, we can show that K=𝒪⁡(1ϵ​log⁡(ϵ−1))K=\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon\sqrt{\log(\epsilon^{-1})}}\big). Using this estimation of KK, we can estimate that 𝔼⁡[𝒯K]=∑k=0Kbk≤σ2δ​∑k=0K(k+s+1)3​log⁡(k+s+1)≤σ2​(K+s+1)4​log⁡(K+s+1)4​δ∼𝒪⁡(1ϵ4​log⁡(ϵ−1))\mathbb{E}\big[\mathcal{T}_{K}\big]=\sum_{k=0}^{K}b_{k}\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\delta}\sum_{k=0}^{K}(k+s+1)^{3}\log(k+s+1)\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}(K+s+1)^{4}\log(K+s+1)}{4\delta}\sim\mathcal{O}\big(\frac{1}{\epsilon^{4}\log(\epsilon^{-1})}\big). C.6 The proof of Proposition 6.1.

We divide the proof of Proposition 6.1 into several steps.

Step 1. First, we show that hh defined in (88) is γ\gamma-strongly convex and LhL_{h}-smooth with Lh:=γ+ν​‖C‖2L_{h}:=\gamma+\nu\|C\|^{2}. Indeed, ∇h​(y)=γ​y+ν​C⊤​tanh⁡(C​y)\nabla h(y)=\gamma y+\nu C^{\top}\tanh(Cy) and ∇2h​(y)=γ​𝕀+ν​C⊤​D​(y)​C\nabla^{2}h(y)=\gamma\mathbb{I}+\nu C^{\top}D(y)C, where D⁡(y):=diag​(sech2⁡(c1⊤​y),⋯,sech2⁡(cr⊤​y))D(y):=\text{diag}\big(\operatorname{sech}^{2}(c_{1}^{\top}y),\cdots,\operatorname{sech}^{2}(c_{r}^{\top}y)\big). Since 0⪯D⁡(y)⪯𝕀0\preceq D(y)\preceq\mathbb{I}, we have

γ​𝕀⪯∇2h​(y)⪯γ​𝕀+ν​C⊤​C⪯(γ+ν​‖C‖2)​𝕀.\gamma\mathbb{I}\preceq\nabla^{2}h(y)\preceq\gamma\mathbb{I}+\nu C^{\top}C\preceq(\gamma+\nu\|C\|^{2})\mathbb{I}.

Hence, hh is γ\gamma-strongly convex and LhL_{h}-smooth with Lh:=γ+ν​‖C‖2L_{h}:=\gamma+\nu\|C\|^{2}.

Step 2. Next, we show that ∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z)\nabla{\tilde{\mathcal{R}}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z) from (90) is 1θ−1\frac{1}{\theta-1}-Lipschitz continuous. The derivative of R~λ,θ\tilde{R}_{\lambda,\theta} is R~λ,θ′(t)=−λ𝟏{t<−θλ}+t+λθ−1𝟏{−θλ≤t<−λ}+t−λθ−1𝟏{λ<t≤θλ}+λ𝟏{t>θλ}\tilde{R}^{\prime}_{\lambda,\theta}(t)=-\lambda\boldsymbol{1}_{\{t<-\theta\lambda\}}+\frac{t+\lambda}{\theta-1}\boldsymbol{1}_{\{-\theta\lambda\leq t<-\lambda\}}+\frac{t-\lambda}{\theta-1}\boldsymbol{1}_{\{\lambda<t\leq\theta\lambda\}}+\lambda\boldsymbol{1}_{\{t>\theta\lambda\}}. It is continuous, monotone nondecreasing, and piece-wise affine, with slope either 00 or 1θ−1\frac{1}{\theta-1}. Therefore, R~λ,θ\tilde{R}_{\lambda,\theta} is convex and continuously differentiable, and ∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z)\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z) is 1θ−1\frac{1}{\theta-1}-Lipschitz continuous.

Step 3. We now prove (i). Let x=(z,y)x=(z,y) and x′=(z′,y′)x^{\prime}=(z^{\prime},y^{\prime}) be arbitrary. By Jensen’s inequality and the LfL_{f}-average smoothness of ff, ff is LfL_{f}-smooth. Thus, by Steps 1–2, one can show that

‖∇f​(z)−∇f​(z′)+B⁡(y−y′)−τ⁡(∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z)−∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z′))‖≤(Lf+τθ−1)|z−z′|+‖B‖​‖y−y′‖,‖∇h​(y)−∇h​(y′)−B⊤​(z−z′)‖≤‖B‖​‖z−z′‖+Lh​‖y−y′‖.\begin{array}[]{llcl}&\|\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(z^{\prime})+B(y-y^{\prime})-\tau(\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z)-\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z^{\prime}))\|&\leq&\big(L_{f}+\frac{\tau}{\theta-1}\big)\|z-z^{\prime}\|+\|B\|\|y-y^{\prime}\|,\\ &\|\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(y^{\prime})-B^{\top}(z-z^{\prime})\|&\leq&\|B\|\|z-z^{\prime}\|+L_{h}\|y-y^{\prime}\|.\end{array}

Therefore, with L~f:=Lf+τθ−1\tilde{L}_{f}:=L_{f}+\frac{\tau}{\theta-1}, we get

[‖[G​x−G​x′]z‖‖[G​x−G​x′]y‖]≤[L~f‖B‖‖B‖Lh]​[‖z−z′‖‖y−y′‖].\begin{array}[]{lcl}\begin{bmatrix}\|[Gx-Gx^{\prime}]_{z}\|\\ \|[Gx-Gx^{\prime}]_{y}\|\end{bmatrix}\leq\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{L}_{f}&\|B\|\\ \|B\|&L_{h}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\|z-z^{\prime}\|\\ \|y-y^{\prime}\|\end{bmatrix}.\end{array}

Hence,

‖G​x−G​x′‖≤‖[L~f‖B‖‖B‖Lh]‖2​‖x−x′‖.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\|Gx-Gx^{\prime}\|\leq\left\|\begin{bmatrix}\tilde{L}_{f}&\|B\|\\ \|B\|&L_{h}\end{bmatrix}\right\|_{2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|.\end{array}

The spectral norm of this symmetric matrix is its largest eigenvalue L:=L~f+Lh+(L~f−Lh)2+4​‖B‖22L:=\frac{\tilde{L}_{f}+L_{h}+\sqrt{(\tilde{L}_{f}-L_{h})^{2}+4\|B\|^{2}}}{2}.

Step 4. Next, we prove (ii). Let x=(z,y)x=(z,y) and x′=(z′,y′)x^{\prime}=(z^{\prime},y^{\prime}), and take w∈Φ​xw\in\Phi x and w′∈Φ​x′w^{\prime}\in\Phi x^{\prime}. By the definition of TT, there exist ξ∈τ​λ​∂‖z‖1+𝒩𝒵​(z)\xi\in\tau\lambda\partial\|z\|_{1}+\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z) and ξ′∈τ​λ​∂‖z′‖1+𝒩𝒵​(z′)\xi^{\prime}\in\tau\lambda\partial\|z^{\prime}\|_{1}+\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{Z}}(z^{\prime}) such that

w=[∇f(z)+By−τ∇ℛ~λ,θ(z)+ξ∇h​(y)−B⊤​z]andw′=[∇f(z′)+By′−τ∇ℛ~λ,θ(z′)+ξ′∇h​(y′)−B⊤​z′].w=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f(z)+By-\tau\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z)+\xi\\ \nabla h(y)-B^{\top}z\end{bmatrix}\quad\text{and}\quad w^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}\nabla f(z^{\prime})+By^{\prime}-\tau\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z^{\prime})+\xi^{\prime}\\ \nabla h(y^{\prime})-B^{\top}z^{\prime}\end{bmatrix}.

Thus,

w−w′=[(∇f​(z)−∇f​(z′))+B⁡(y−y′)−τ⁡(∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z)−∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z′))+(ξ−ξ′)(∇h​(y)−∇h​(y′))−B⊤​(z−z′)].w-w^{\prime}=\begin{bmatrix}\big(\nabla f(z)-\nabla f(z^{\prime})\big)+B(y-y^{\prime})-\tau\big(\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z)-\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z^{\prime})\big)+(\xi-\xi^{\prime})\\ \big(\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(y^{\prime}))-B^{\top}(z-z^{\prime})\end{bmatrix}. (107)

Taking its inner product with x−x′x-x^{\prime} and using the convexity of ff, the monotonicity of τλ∂∥⋅∥1+∂δ𝒵\tau\lambda\partial\|\cdot\|_{1}+\partial\delta_{\mathcal{Z}}, and Steps 1–2, we obtain

⟨w−w′,x−x′⟩≥−τθ−1​‖z−z′‖2+γ​‖y−y′‖2.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle w-w^{\prime},x-x^{\prime}\rangle&\geq&-\frac{\tau}{\theta-1}\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2}+\gamma\|y-y^{\prime}\|^{2}.\end{array} (108)

We consider two cases.

  • •

    Case 1. If ⟨w−w′,x−x′⟩≥0\langle w-w^{\prime},x-x^{\prime}\rangle\geq 0, then the desired co-hypomonotonicity inequality holds trivially.

  • •

    Case 2. If ⟨w−w′,x−x′⟩<0\langle w-w^{\prime},x-x^{\prime}\rangle<0, then (108) implies ‖y−y′‖2≤τγ⁡(θ−1)​‖z−z′‖2\|y-y^{\prime}\|^{2}\leq\frac{\tau}{\gamma(\theta-1)}\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2}. Hence, using σ:=σmin​(B⊤)\sigma:=\sigma_{\min}(B^{\top}) and the LhL_{h}-smoothness of hh,

    ‖w−w′‖≥‖(∇h​(y)−∇h​(y′))−B⊤​(z−z′)‖≥σ​‖z−z′‖−Lh​‖y−y′‖≥(σ−Lh​(τγ⁡(θ−1))1/2)​‖z−z′‖>0.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\|w-w^{\prime}\|&\geq&\|\big(\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(y^{\prime}))-B^{\top}(z-z^{\prime})\|\\ &\geq&\sigma\|z-z^{\prime}\|-L_{h}\|y-y^{\prime}\|\\ &\geq&\big(\sigma-L_{h}\big(\frac{\tau}{\gamma(\theta-1)}\big)^{1/2}\big)\|z-z^{\prime}\|>0.\end{array}

    Combining this estimate with (108) gives

    ⟨w−w′,x−x′⟩≥−τθ−1​‖z−z′‖2≥−τ(θ−1)​(σ−Lh​τ/((θ−1)​γ))2​‖w−w′‖2.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\langle w-w^{\prime},x-x^{\prime}\rangle&\geq&-\frac{\tau}{\theta-1}\|z-z^{\prime}\|^{2}\geq-\frac{\tau}{(\theta-1)\left(\sigma-L_{h}\sqrt{\tau/((\theta-1)\gamma)}\right)^{2}}\|w-w^{\prime}\|^{2}.\end{array}

    Thus, the desired inequality holds with ρ:=τ(θ−1)​(σ−Lh​τ/((θ−1)​γ))2\rho:=\frac{\tau}{(\theta-1)\left(\sigma-L_{h}\sqrt{\tau/((\theta-1)\gamma)}\right)^{2}}.

Therefore, Φ:=G+T\Phi:=G+T is globally ρ\rho-co-hypomonotone.

Step 5. Finally, we prove (iii). By Minkowski’s inequality, the 1θ−1\frac{1}{\theta-1}-Lipschitz continuity of ∇ℛ~λ,θ\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}, and the average smoothness of ff, for L~f:=Lf+τθ−1\tilde{L}_{f}:=L_{f}+\frac{\tau}{\theta-1}, we can show that

[1n​∑i=1n‖∇fi​(z)−∇fi​(z′)+B⁡(y−y′)−τ⁡(∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z)−∇ℛ~λ,θ​(z′))‖2]1/2≤L~f|z−z′|+‖B‖​‖y−y′‖.\begin{array}[]{lcl}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\nabla f_{i}(z)-\nabla f_{i}(z^{\prime})+B(y-y^{\prime})-\tau(\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z)-\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{R}}_{\lambda,\theta}(z^{\prime}))\|^{2}\right]^{1/2}{\!\!\!}\leq\tilde{L}_{f}\|z-z^{\prime}\|+\|B\|\|y-y^{\prime}\|.\end{array}

Arguing as in Step 3 gives

1n​∑i=1n‖Gi​x−Gi​x′‖2≤L2​‖x−x′‖2,\begin{array}[]{lcl}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|G_{i}x-G_{i}x^{\prime}\|^{2}\leq L^{2}\|x-x^{\prime}\|^{2},\end{array} (109)

where L=L~f+Lh+(L~f−Lh)2+4​‖B‖22L=\frac{\tilde{L}_{f}+L_{h}+\sqrt{(\tilde{L}_{f}-L_{h})^{2}+4\|B\|^{2}}}{2}.

We next bound ‖x−x′‖\|x-x^{\prime}\| by ‖w−w′‖\|w-w^{\prime}\|. It is easy to show that ∇h​(y)−∇h​(y′)=Q⁡(y−y′)\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(y^{\prime})=Q(y-y^{\prime}), where Q:=∫01∇2h​(y′+t⁡(y−y′))​𝑑tQ:=\int_{0}^{1}\nabla^{2}h(y^{\prime}+t(y-y^{\prime}))\mathrm{d}t satisfies γ​𝕀⪯Q⪯Lh​𝕀\gamma\mathbb{I}\preceq Q\preceq L_{h}\mathbb{I}. Thus, from the second block of (107), we get

y−y′=Q−1([w−w′]y+B⊤(z−z′)),1Lh𝕀⪯Q−1⪯1γ𝕀.\begin{array}[]{lcl}y-y^{\prime}=Q^{-1}\big([w-w^{\prime}]_{y}+B^{\top}(z-z^{\prime})\big),\qquad\frac{1}{L_{h}}\mathbb{I}\preceq Q^{-1}\preceq\frac{1}{\gamma}\mathbb{I}.\end{array} (110)

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
